cleared.check: Exits on Robinhood Chain: can an ordinary account, including one on the restricted list, make the transaction filter reject or fail a transaction of another user on a pool without attacker-made hook or token.
cleared.result: No path found. A transaction is filtered for the addresses it touches itself, and cycle 2 showed that a swap or removal on such a pool calls only the PoolManager, the router, the tokens and the recipient the user chose. Two neighbour effects exist in the client and neither reaches other users today. Before v3.11.0 a filtered transaction caused the sequencer to reject clean transactions behind it in the same block, and the changelog records the fix. A user transaction is rolled back together with the redeems it scheduled when one of them touches a filtered address, and the group never includes another user's transaction. The on-chain list holds transaction hashes that only the filterer account can add. The live build v3.13.0-rc.9 is not public, so I could not confirm that the v3.11.0 fix is unchanged in it.

cleared.check: A2 and A5 for USDG on Robinhood Chain, which pays claimable rewards: can an ordinary account raise balanceOf(PoolManager) without a transfer, enrol the PoolManager, or earn rewards with USDG borrowed from the PoolManager inside one transaction. The PoolManager holds 16.83M USDG.
cleared.result: No. balanceOf returns the stored balance and rewards are paid only by a claim, which is a transfer from the claim source to a destination named by the claimer or manager of a payout group. The PoolManager is in no payout group and has no pending proposal. Enrolment needs the registrar role, or a proposal by a group's claimer that the account itself accepts by calling acceptRegisterRewardAddress, or a signature of the account that a claimer presents while partner signed registration is switched on. The PoolManager cannot make that call and cannot sign, and partner signed registration is switched off. The multiplier changes only when a daily period boundary passes, and block.timestamp is constant inside a transaction, so shares bought and sold in one transaction earn nothing. A take and return of USDG inside one unlock therefore yields no reward to the borrower. The registrar could enrol the PoolManager. Rewards on its balance would then go to that group's destination and its balance would stay unchanged. That is an issuer action and falls under F-002. I matched the deployed contract to the repository by selectors and views and did not compare bytecode.

cleared.check: Exits, token limits: does globalTransferSettings() on USDG set a transfer volume or rate limit that an attacker could use up with USDG borrowed from the PoolManager, which would make later payouts from the PoolManager revert.
cleared.result: No. The five fields are the reference time and period of the reward multiplier, the switch for partner signed registration, a reserved gap and the pause flag. _transfer reverts only for a zero recipient, a frozen party, an insufficient balance, a pause or an overflow of the packed 64 bit fields, and 64 bits hold 18 trillion USDG. The pause and freeze switches belong to the issuer (F-002).

cleared.check: Known weaknesses of the last two years in Nitro, ArbOS and the two newer chains, beyond the items cycle 2 cleared: can an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: None applies. The Trail of Bits review of ArbOS 60 and 61 has one high finding, a map iteration order that can split consensus, and eight informational ones about gas pricing constraints and an error path of the filter. None moves balances. The retryable ordering hazard that Trail of Bits described in 2024 concerns contracts that send several dependent retryables, and the only parent chain messages the PoolManager depends on are single owner calls. The Stylus bugs behind the activation pause affect liveness according to the Security Council. The two incidents reported on Robinhood Chain were an accounting bug inside an exchange and trading ahead of a bridge solver, both outside the PoolManager. For Elysium I found a third party commentary and no published audit report of its own bridge contracts, and its documentation lists audits among later steps. Timestamps that repeat across blocks, which that commentary notes, do not matter to code that reads no block field.

EIP-7702 says that CALL loads the code at the delegated address and executes it in the context of the authority, and EIP-7 says that the call created by DELEGATECALL has the same sender and value as the original call. cleared.check: Leads L-153 and L-202 for Celo: does the fee currency debit or credit, or any other client feature, run code inside a call in progress under a transient storage map separate from the caller's while keeping its transfers and storage writes.
cleared.result: No. The debit and the credit are steps of the transaction handler and run before the first frame of the main call and after its last frame has returned. A contract cannot start them. The debit starts from the empty map of a new transaction and the handler clears its transient writes before the main call (handler.rs lines 695 to 698). The credit runs on the same journal as the main call and clears transient storage when it ends (core_contracts.rs lines 241 to 248). The fee currency must be registered in FeeCurrencyDirectory, which Governance owns, so the code that runs is not chosen by the caller. The other system calls of the client read exchange rates through call_read_only, which reverts everything it did. unlock is one call frame (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so neither step can separate a take from its debit.

cleared.check: Lead L-203 on both chains: can a call frame carry value that the caller's balance did not lose in the same journal (fee currency transactions and deposits with mint on Celo, gasless transactions and deposits on X Layer, the transfer precompile).
cleared.result: No. On Celo a fee currency transaction is rejected when its value exceeds the sender's native balance, a deposit's mint is added to the sender before execution, and the value then moves in the call frame (handler.rs lines 773 and 805 to 815). The transfer precompile uses the journal transfer and halts on an error, and it accepts only the CELO token as caller (transfer.rs lines 52 to 57 and 91 to 125). On X Layer a gasless transaction is rejected when the sender balance is below the value and the balance is otherwise left as it is, and a deposit adds its mint first (handler.rs lines 113 to 143 and 178 to 188). The one branch that raises a balance to the value runs only with the balance check disabled, which block production does not use. A native credit in core is msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354), and on both chains that value has left the caller's balance.

cleared.check: On-chain differential for value semantics. A probe contract placed by state override made a CALL with 5 wei, a CALLCODE with 3 wei and a DELEGATECALL to a second probe that returns CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE and BALANCE(CALLER). Runs: funded sender with value 7, funded sender with value 0, and an unfunded probe.
cleared.result: All 21 endpoints returned the Ethereum result. The CALL moved exactly 5 wei from caller to callee and the callee read CALLVALUE 5. The CALLCODE frame read CALLVALUE 3 with the caller's balance unchanged. The DELEGATECALL frame read the parent's CALLVALUE with no balance change. From an account with balance 0 the CALL and the CALLCODE with value failed. On Tempo the run with transaction value was rejected with 'value transfer not allowed' and the run with an overridden balance behaved as on Ethereum. CALLCODE and DELEGATECALL frames show value without a debit on every client by design. cleared.result: No path for an ordinary account. An ETH deposit mints to the sender and moves the amount with core.Transfer without running the EVM, so no contract sees CALLVALUE. cleared.check: Lead L-166, method for all 21 networks. For each candidate address X the stub at the PoolManager address reads X.balanceOf(PoolManager), makes one call to X and reads the balance again, in one eth_call. Four shapes per X: a value call of 10^12 wei with empty calldata, a zero value call with empty calldata, transfer(recipient, 0) and transfer(recipient, 1). Candidates: the ERC-4337 EntryPoints v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8 on every chain, the wrapped native token, every address with code from 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 00ff on the ten OP Stack chains, the system contracts of BNB Smart Chain and Polygon, the Avalanche and HyperEVM precompile ranges, liquid staking tokens, and the 248 largest pooled tokens.
cleared.result: The addresses whose balanceOf(PoolManager) rose on the value call are the wrapped native token of each chain (exactly 10^12 for 10^12 wei on all 20 chains that have native value), the three EntryPoints (exactly 10^12; on Tempo they have code and the value call fails, because the chain has no native value), stETH on Ethereum (999,999,999,999), wstETH on Ethereum (800,071,968,325), sAVAX on Avalanche (771,425,961,435) and qiAVAX on Avalanche (4,276 units of 8 decimals). No address raised the ledger on a zero value call or on a zero amount transfer. The EntryPoints reject transfer(address,uint256), so a credit under their id can only become a claim. For the others the full cycle with A = 10^12 wei is: sync(X) stores B (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288); take(address(0), X, A) sets the caller's delta under address(0) to minus A and sends A to X (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295, src/types/Currency.sol:48); X books r times A to the PoolManager; settle credits the caller r times A under id X (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364); take(X, caller, r times A) pays that out; the caller then pays A with msg.value to clear the native debt, because unlock needs every delta at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The PoolManager's native balance and its X balance end where they started. The caller paid A and holds what a direct deposit of A into X mints, less 1 wei of rounding for stETH. No part of the cycle uses value that belonged to pools.

The gas price was 25 gwei, so 100,000 gas for one round costs 2.5 * 10^15 wei, more than 2,500 times the largest gain. cleared.check: Zero amount and dust transfers with the PoolManager as sender, for the largest pooled tokens of each network. Token lists: explorer balances of the PoolManager ranked by value on OP Mainnet, Unichain, World Chain, Ink, Soneium, Celo and MegaETH (Blockscout), on Ethereum and Avalanche (Routescan), the largest currencies of Uniswap v4 pools by tracked reserve on Base, Arbitrum One, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Monad, X Layer, Zora, Tempo, Arc, Robinhood Chain and Elysium (GeckoTerminal), and a hand list on HyperEVM. 248 tokens, 9 to 16 per chain. For each token: transfer(recipient, 0), transfer(recipient, 1), transfer(PoolManager, 0), a transfer of one thousandth of the balance to a plain recipient, to the PoolManager itself, to the token address and to the zero address, with the sender balance read before and after and the gas of the inner call measured. On 13 endpoints the logs of the zero amount transfer were read with eth_simulateV1.
cleared.result: In every successful call the sender balance changed by exactly the amount sent: zero for a zero amount, zero for a transfer to itself, minus the amount otherwise. No token paid a reward, released vested tokens, rebased, changed a delegation or charged the sender a fee on these calls, and no call moved a second token to or from the PoolManager in the logs. Exceptions and side effects, all without a gain for the caller: G$ on Celo and ELO and v4CRCL on Elysium and X Layer revert (see findings). sAVAX rejects a zero amount transfer with TRANSFER_ZERO_VALUE, so take(sAVAX, to, 0) reverts. stETH moves nothing for 1 wei while the caller is debited 1. qiAVAX runs Benqi reward accounting (see finding). The stock tokens on Robinhood Chain emit TransferWithScaledUI, SPCXB on BNB Smart Chain emits TransferWithUIAmount and ANTX on Ink emits TransferShares next to Transfer, with no balance effect beyond the amount. Vote tokens (OP, UNI, ARB, AAVE) used under 13,000 gas, which leaves no room for a checkpoint write, as expected for a holder without a delegate. USDT on Ethereum returns no data, which the success test accepts (src/types/Currency.sol:68). The largest zero amount gas figures were 140,444 (qiAVAX), about 106,000 on Monad for the wrapped stock tokens, whose contract on Ink uses 36,094 and logs only Transfer, and 40,713 (SPCXB). On the 8 endpoints without eth_simulateV1 (World Chain, Celo, X Layer, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Arc, HyperEVM) the statement about second tokens rests on the gas figures and on the balance of the token itself. The lists are samples of 9 to 16 tokens per chain and do not cover every pooled token.

cleared.check: USDSC on Soneium (1.90 million held) and mUSD on Monad (1.88 million held) are yield bearing dollar tokens with a public claim function. Does a claim raise the PoolManager balance, which a caller could book between sync and settle?
cleared.result: No. Both contracts answer yieldRecipient() with one fixed address (0xda798684ffd5eb509c2ab7b8352ec55b31f18201 and 0x4177a5287fae4767311dad02547b57d1b8cf5fbf) and yield() with the amount waiting for it. They do not answer accruedYieldOf, isEarning or claimRecipientFor for the PoolManager. The yield goes to the one recipient, and the PoolManager balance moves only by transfers. USDM, CUSD, apxUSD, AUSD, USDG on three chains, stcUSD, eUSD and WBRL answer none of the eleven yield or reward selectors I tried.

cleared.check: Can take make the PoolManager call itself with effect, so that its own ERC-6909 ledger serves as a mirrored ledger?
cleared.result: No. take calls transfer(address,uint256) on the currency address and sync calls balanceOf(address) (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75, 94). The ERC-6909 functions of the PoolManager are transfer(address,uint256,uint256) and the getter balanceOf(address,uint256) (src/ERC6909.sol:17, 25), which have other selectors, and the contract has no fallback or receive function (the only payable functions are settle and settleFor, src/PoolManager.sol:300-307). A take or sync that names the PoolManager as currency reverts, and a native take to the PoolManager reverts.

cleared.check: What the two dangerous shapes would do to this code, so that each network can be judged against them. Shape A: an inner run that starts with an empty transient map and whose storage writes and token transfers are kept. Shape B: an inner run, or a rollback, that drops transient writes while keeping storage writes and token transfers. Walked through unlock, sync, settle, settleFor, take, mint and burn.
cleared.result: The code has no defence of its own against either shape, so the answer rests on the chain. Shape A: sync needs no lock and stores the currency and the balance in two transient slots (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). An inner run that sees no unlock flag (src/libraries/Lock.sol:23-27) can call unlock itself (src/PoolManager.sol:105-107), sync, pay, settle and mint a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), and end with its own counter at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The outer run still holds the older reserves value, so its settle measures the same balance rise again (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360) and credits it a second time. Shape B: take writes the debit to a transient slot and then transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:32-40). If the debit and the counter increment (src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:18-24) are dropped while the transfer is kept, unlock passes its check at src/PoolManager.sol:112 with the tokens gone. The reverse of shape B, where transient writes survive a rollback that undoes a token transfer, lets a settle credit (src/PoolManager.sol:364) outlive the payment. burn and settleFor follow the same pattern (src/PoolManager.sol:305-307, 332-336). Calls that follow one another at the top level of one transaction (a Tempo type 0x76 batch, the phases of a Base type 0x79 transaction, user operations of one bundle) do not produce either shape: unlock opens and closes inside one call frame (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so between two top-level calls the flag is false and every delta is zero, and only the synced currency and reserves can carry over, which earlier cycles cleared. The remaining items of this file answer, network by network, whether shape A or B exists. No network has one that an ordinary contract can start from inside a call.

cleared.check: On-chain test on all 21 RPC endpoints: does a call from an inner frame to any precompile, predeploy or system address change the caller's transient storage. One 3,640 byte creation payload, sent with eth_call and no to address, stores 0xaa55 in transient slot 1, then calls each of 173 addresses three ways with 20,000 gas (3,000 on HyperEVM): CALL with empty calldata, CALL with transfer(address,uint256), STATICCALL with balanceOf(address). It returns the slot and the loop counter.
cleared.result: All 21 endpoints returned 0xaa55 and a count of 173. The address list holds the standard precompiles 0x01 to 0x11 and 0x100, the OP Stack predeploys 0x4200..00 to 0x4200..2f, the ArbOS precompiles 0x64 to 0x74 with 0xc8, 0xff and 0xa4b05, the Celo transfer precompile 0xfd and the CELO token, sixteen Tempo precompile and TIP-20 addresses, the Arc range 0x1800..00 to 0x1800..09 and 0x3600..00, the HyperEVM range 0x0800 to 0x0813 with 0x2222..22, 0x3333..33 and 0x5555..55, the BNB Smart Chain and Polygon system contracts 0x1000 to 0x1008, 0x2000 to 0x2006, 0x3000 and 0x1010, the MegaETH system contracts 0x6342..00 to 0x6342..05, the Avalanche ranges 0x0100..00 to 02 and 0x0200..00 to 05, and the two Base precompiles 0x8130..aa01 and aa02. The test uses zeroed arguments, so it shows that no special address resets or replaces the transient map on a plain call. It does not exercise the function of each precompile. The items below cover the features that take specific input.

cleared.check: On-chain test on all 21 RPC endpoints: is transient storage restored on every way a frame can fail, and is it restored to the earlier nonzero value. The earlier critic probe covered REVERT. This probe creates a child contract and calls it so that the child writes transient slot 1 and then ends with REVERT, with INVALID, by running out of gas in a loop, and with REVERT after a nested call that itself succeeded and wrote slot 2. It then lets a write succeed, repeats the reverting call, and runs the same writes through DELEGATECALL against the parent's own slot.
cleared.result: All 21 endpoints returned the same 15 words: slot 1 and slot 2 read zero after each of the four failures, slot 1 reads 0x55 after the successful write and still 0x55 after a later reverted write of 0x11, and the parent's slot reads 0xaa after a reverted and after an INVALID delegatecall and 0x55 after a successful one. A settle credit or a take debit written in a frame that fails is therefore undone together with the token transfer of that frame on every network, including the clients that do not use revm or go-ethereum (Tempo with evm2, Monad, HyperEVM). The result describes the RPC node of each network.

cleared.check: Tempo. Type 0x76 batches, precompiles that might call out to contracts, the storage credit settlement that removes transient slots, T14 configurable accounts and the zone contracts. For each: can a contract start it from inside a call, which transient map does it use, and are transient writes journaled like storage writes.
cleared.result: No feature gives a second transient map. The mainnet node reports tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97, and the manifest at that commit pins evm2 at revision 66687c18 (the main branch pins e25a95fb today, which is the revision an earlier cleared item quoted). A type 0x76 batch runs every call as a top-level frame with the signer as caller under one checkpoint (handler.rs lines 1277 to 1372, checkpoint at 1289, rollback at 1339), and the calls share one transient map that is not cleared between them. An ordinary contract cannot start a batch. evm2 keeps one transient map per transaction (state/mod.rs line 59), journals each TSTORE (lines 806 to 836), restores it in rollback (lines 891 to 898) and clears it in clear_transaction_state (lines 523 to 539). Every call frame and every precompile call takes a checkpoint from that journal and rolls back on failure (evm/mod.rs lines 1691 to 1795). Tempo precompiles run native code through a storage provider that offers sload, sstore, tload, tstore, events and checkpoints and has no function that calls a contract (precompiles/src/storage/mod.rs lines 92 to 280, dispatch at precompiles/src/lib.rs lines 309 to 342), so no precompile runs caller-chosen code. take_transient_storage removes slots part way through settlement, and its only caller passes the storage credits address 0x1060..00 (state/mod.rs lines 842 to 859, handler/config.rs lines 444 to 455), so PoolManager slots are untouched. T14 is not active on mainnet: eth_getCode at 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 returned 0x near block 50341036 while the T7 and T8 precompiles return 0xef. The specification of TIP-1107 registers a configurable account before any call runs and outside the rollback checkpoint, and the code does the same (handler.rs line 1693), so it is a top-level step that touches no PoolManager state. Zone contracts are ordinary EVM bytecode on the main chain (ZonePortal implementation 23,994 bytes at 0x5AD1..00, ZoneMessenger 1,858 bytes at 0x5A4D..00, and nextZoneId() on the factory returned 4), so a callback from them is an ordinary call on the same journal, and the zone itself is a separate chain where this PoolManager does not exist. Not confirmed: whether validators run the evm2 JIT backend, and whether its TSTORE path matches the interpreter. Both probes above passed on the public RPC node.

cleared.check: Base. Type 0x79 Base Transactions, the B20, policy, nonce and transaction context precompiles, and validity transactions. Can any of them run caller-chosen code under another transient map, or drop transient writes while keeping storage writes.
cleared.result: No. The node reports base/v1.5.6 on reth v2.5.2 and that release builds on revm 42. Type 0x79 belongs to the Everest upgrade, which the Base upgrade page lists with no date for Sepolia or mainnet, and the latest mainnet block held only types 0x7e, 0x2 and 0x0. In the v1.5.6 source each phase takes one journal checkpoint, a failed phase is reverted through it and a completed phase is committed (eip8130.rs lines 1260 to 1344). revm restores transient storage in checkpoint_revert, so a reverted phase loses its transient writes together with its storage writes and transfers. The specification states that every call is dispatched from the sender, so phases are top-level calls and no contract can start one. Phases of one transaction share the transient map, which gives the sender nothing beyond what a contract with several calls has. The Base precompiles reach state through a provider with sload, sstore, tload, tstore, events and checkpoints and no function that calls a contract (precompile-storage/src/provider.rs lines 34 to 140). Validity transactions add inclusion conditions and no execution context.

cleared.check: Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium. Stylus host calls, retryable redeems started with ArbRetryableTx.redeem from inside a call, and the group rollback of the sequencer. Does any of them execute code under a transient map other than the one of the running transaction, or undo transient writes apart from storage writes.
cleared.result: No. A Stylus program reaches other contracts through closures that call evm.Call, evm.DelegateCall and evm.StaticCall on the EVM that is already running (arbos/programs/api.go lines 186 to 190), and its transient host calls read and write the same StateDB under the acting address (lines 119 to 127). A contract called by a Stylus program therefore sees the PoolManager's lock flag and deltas as any other callee does. redeem only emits RedeemScheduled. The node builds the retry transaction from that log after the scheduling transaction has finished and appends it to the queue as its own transaction (tx_processor.go lines 924 to 950, block_processor.go line 719), and an earlier cleared item showed that every transaction starts with StateDB.Prepare. The group rollback saves a checkpoint for a user transaction and the redeems it scheduled and restores whole transactions (block_processor.go lines 125 to 134 and 583 to 594), so storage, balances and transient state go back together. Not confirmed: Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain report nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 at commit b72783f, and neither that tag nor that commit is served by raw.githubusercontent.com. I read master and v3.12.0, whose api.go has the same call sites. Elysium reports a locally built binary. Both probes above passed on all three RPC nodes.

cleared.check: MegaETH. The KeylessDeploy sandbox is the one feature on the 21 networks with shape A: it runs caller-chosen init code in a second EVM with a new journal over live state and merges the resulting state into the parent. Can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call, and is transient state merged back.
cleared.result: It cannot be started from inside a call, and transient state is not merged. The interceptor returns without acting when the call is inside a sandbox or its depth is not zero (system/intercept.rs lines 295 to 303). The sandbox builds a new context over a database wrapper and runs one transaction in it (sandbox/execution.rs lines 583 to 650), and the sandbox sources never copy transient storage in either direction, so the inner run starts empty and its transient values are dropped. On the public RPC node near block 32592160, eth_call straight to 0x6342000000000000000000000000000000000003 with keylessDeploy(bytes,uint256) and a one byte payload reverted with 0xae1270d3, which is MalformedEncoding() and shows interception at depth zero. The same calldata sent from a creation frame, one level down, failed with return data 0x1894f076, which is NotIntercepted(), the revert of the Solidity stub. A sandbox is therefore the first frame of a transaction whose target is the KeylessDeploy address. The parent has run no contract code before it and runs none after it, so the PoolManager has no transient state in the parent that the sandbox could bypass, and inside the sandbox unlock, sync, settle and take share one map. The latest block held transaction types 0x7e, 0x0 and 0x2, each of which has one top-level call. I did not enumerate the transaction types the node accepts, and the lead below asks for that. Not confirmed: which mega-evm revision mega-reth v2.2.3 pins. I read the main branch, version 1.7.3, and the on-chain result agrees with it.

cleared.check: Arc. On-chain test of the CallFrom precompile at 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000003: does the child call it starts see the transient storage of the surrounding transaction, and are the child's transient writes kept. Earlier cycles answered from the main branch source only.
cleared.result: The child runs on the same map. With state overrides I placed a probe at the Multicall3From address 0x522fAf9A91c41c443c66765030741e4AaCe147D0, which is one of the two callers the precompile accepts, and a counter contract at a second address. The counter returns its transient slot 2 and adds 0x22 to it. The probe called the counter directly, then through callFrom, then directly again. The three readings were 0, 0x22 and 0x44 near block 32640276, both with the helper and with tx.origin as the substituted sender. An empty map for the child would give 0 as the second reading, and dropped child writes would give 0x22 as the third. The same probe at an address outside the allowlist failed at the precompile call. The source agrees: init_subcall rejects callers outside the allowlist, static context, value and a sender that is neither the caller nor the transaction signer, and pushes the child onto the same frame stack with a checkpoint from the same journal (evm.rs lines 884 to 952 and 1031 to 1040), and a failed child is rolled back through that checkpoint (lines 1228 to 1231).

cleared.check: Celo. The fee currency calls debitGasFees and creditGasFees that the node makes around a CIP-64 transaction. Can a contract start them, which transient map do they use, and is anything discarded between them and the main call.
cleared.result: They are node calls at the top level and use the map of the transaction. The sequencer RPC reports the op-geth fork at commit c7ed55b8. In that source innerExecute calls StateDB.Prepare, which replaces the transient map, at state_transition.go line 602, and the debit runs after it inside preCheck at line 605. The credit runs after the main call has returned (line 824). Both go through evm.CallWithABI on the same EVM and StateDB (contracts/fee_currencies.go lines 88 and 154). Nothing clears transient storage between the debit, the main call and the credit, and no opcode or precompile lets a contract trigger either call. By the time the credit runs, unlock has returned or the main call has reverted, so the flag is false and all deltas are zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112-113). The fee currency is chosen from the governance list, so no caller-chosen code runs in these calls. Whether a listed token calls out to untrusted code during credit stays with the open lead of the Celo unit.

cleared.check: HyperEVM. The sendToEvmWithData action that makes the node call coreReceiveWithData on a linked contract, and CoreWriter. Can an ordinary contract start either from inside a call so that code runs under another transient map.
cleared.result: No, on the documentation and the public clients. sendToEvmWithData is an action signed on HyperCore and posted to the exchange endpoint. The documentation describes Core to EVM transfers as credited by a system transaction that calls the linked contract as the system address. A system transaction is a transaction of its own, and earlier cycles read in the archive client that each one runs through a single transact call with transient storage cleared at its end. The inner run therefore starts with an empty map because it is a different transaction, and no PoolManager unlock can be open around it. A contract on HyperEVM cannot start one within its own call: transfers back to HyperCore are picked up from Transfer logs after execution, as the documentation states, and CoreWriter at 0x3333333333333333333333333333333333333333 emits a log that HyperCore processes as an action after execution, with a delay of a few seconds for some actions. Both probes above passed on the RPC node, including the calls to 0x3333333333333333333333333333333333333333 and 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222. Not confirmed: the validator binary is closed, so the statement that no in-call path exists rests on documentation, on the archive client and on these probes.

cleared.check: Monad. Whether optimistic parallel execution, the call frame model of the client or the staking precompile gives a call a transient map of its own, and whether a failed frame restores transient storage together with storage.
cleared.result: No. Transient storage is a field of the per-account state object next to storage (account_state.hpp line 70, accessors at lines 126 to 154). The state keeps a version stack per account: entering a frame pushes a version, a write copies the account state into the new version, pop_accept folds it into the parent and pop_reject drops it (state.cpp lines 129 to 183, version_stack.hpp). Storage and transient storage of an account are therefore kept or dropped by the same operation. An earlier cleared item showed that each execution attempt of a transaction builds a new State. The staking contract source contains no call into the EVM host, and precompiles.cpp dispatches only the standard precompiles, so no precompile runs caller-chosen code. Both probes above passed on the RPC node. I did not read the JIT compiler's TSTORE path.

cleared.check: Avalanche. The nativeAssetCall precompile at 0x0100000000000000000000000000000000000002 transfers an Avalanche native asset and then calls an address chosen by the caller, keeping the original caller as msg.sender. Is it active, and which state does its inner call use.
cleared.result: It is switched off, and it used the same state when it was active. From the Banff rules on, all three native asset addresses map to DeprecatedContract, whose Run returns ErrExecutionReverted (params/hooks_libevm.go lines 113 to 122, nativeasset/contract.go line 178). eth_call to the address with 84 zero bytes on the public endpoint returned execution reverted. The earlier implementation took a StateDB snapshot and called env.Call on the running EVM (nativeasset/contract.go lines 146 to 171), so its callee shared the transient map of the transaction. The endpoint reports avalanchego 1.15.3, the release I read. No other C-Chain precompile takes a call target.

cleared.check: Polygon and BNB Smart Chain. Can a precompile or a system contract path run caller-chosen code with a separate transient map, and does the parallel executor of Bor give a task a map that outlives the task.
cleared.result: No. In Bor v2.11.0 and in BSC v1.8.2 (the version the BSC endpoint reports) a precompile implements RequiredGas, Run(input) and Name, and Run receives only the input bytes (core/vm/contracts.go lines 51 to 55 and 56 to 60), so a precompile has no handle on the EVM and cannot start a call. Both clients replace the transient map in StateDB.Prepare (Bor statedb.go line 3051, BSC statedb.go line 1532). Bor's parallel tasks run ApplyMessage, which calls Prepare, on a state object of their own (parallel_state_processor.go lines 101 to 150 and 451). State sync records and Parlia system transactions run at the top level between user transactions, as earlier cycles recorded. A public Polygon endpoint reports bor v2.11.1-private, one patch above the source I read. Both probes above passed on both networks.

cleared.check: World Chain and X Layer. PBH bundles, and the node additions of both chains that I could locate (the World Chain EVM crate and the X Layer bridge intercept crate). Does any of them run user code in a context of its own inside a transaction.
cleared.result: No. A PBH transaction is a standard OP transaction that targets the PBHEntryPoint contract, and a PBH bundle is a standard ERC-4337 bundle, so every user operation runs as a nested call of one transaction on one journal. The builder checks proofs and orders transactions. The World Chain manifest at tag v2.8.2, the version the endpoint reports, pins revm 43.0.2, and the EVM crate on the main branch holds configuration, an EVM factory, execution wiring and caches, and its lib.rs and factory.rs name no precompile. The X Layer intercept crate inspects the logs of a finished transaction in the payload builder and drops the whole transaction when a bridge event matches, which is a decision about inclusion. The gasless rule of X Layer was covered by an earlier cleared item and I did not read it again. Both nodes keep the revm journal, where transient storage is cleared in commit_tx, discard_tx and finalize and restored in checkpoint_revert (journal/inner.rs lines 141 to 250 and 622 to 638). Both probes above passed on both networks. I did not read every crate of either node.

cleared.check: Ethereum and the OP Stack chains without node additions (OP Mainnet, Unichain, Zora, Ink, Soneium). EIP-7702 delegated accounts, ERC-4337 bundles, deposit transactions, and any frame style transaction type. Is there an execution context with its own transient map inside a transaction.
cleared.result: No. EIP-1153 defines transient storage as discarded after every transaction and shared by all frames of the transaction. Delegated code under EIP-7702 runs in an ordinary frame at the account's address, and an ERC-4337 bundle is one transaction that calls the EntryPoint contract, so both use the one map. cleared.check: Lead L-171: are L1 deposits placed ahead of sequencer transactions, and can a deposit be skipped because the block's state growth counter has reached 1,000 while deposits remain?
cleared.result: Deposits come first. In 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks the user deposit is at index 1, after the L1 attributes transaction and before every system and sequencer transaction, so the counter is near zero when deposits run. The OP Stack derivation rule places the user deposits of an L1 block in the first L2 block of its epoch. The L1 portal sells at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block, and cycle 2 measured 20,333,678 gas for 900 new slots, so the deposits of one L1 block cannot create 1,000 entries. The limiter also applies its test before a transaction and admits the one that reaches the limit. A deposit can fail on its own transaction limits and is then included as failed with its mint kept.

The documented transaction types are legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-7702 and deposit, each with one top-level call, and a delegated account whose code points at KeylessDeploy has a different target address, so the interceptor does not match it. cleared.result: No such rule exists in mega-evm. The handler hook before_run treats only transactions sent from the system address specially and restricts them to the Oracle contract (evm/execution.rs lines 87 to 157, system/tx.rs line 25). The block executor passes deposits through the same limiter as other transactions and exempts them from the data availability tests (block/executor.rs lines 489 to 530, block/limit.rs lines 822 and 924). The files contain no list of blocked senders or targets. A deposit fails only on the per transaction resource limits that apply to every transaction. The payload builder of mega-reth is closed source and was not read.

Sixteen call shapes (P1 with value 1 wei and with zero value, P2 transfer of 0 and of 1, P3 balanceOf under STATICCALL, the ten IHooks selectors of P5 and unlockCallback of P7) against 45 targets: precompiles 0x05 to 0x0a, read precompiles 0x0800 to 0x0814, the HYPE bridge address, CoreWriter, WHYPE, the CoreDepositWallet, USDC, the AQAv2 treasury address, the USDC system address, the system interest address, three EntryPoints, Multicall3, Permit2, the deterministic deployer, CreateX, the PoolManager owner, PositionManager and the zero address.

cleared.check: Which system transactions can an ordinary HyperCore account cause, which need a validator vote, and can any of them reach the PoolManager or carry it as sender (assumptions A2 and A8, the question the cycle 2 critic left with F-020 and F-044)?
cleared.result: An ordinary account can cause three kinds: a HYPE credit from the bridge address to an EVM account, a transfer call on a linked contract from that token's system address, and a coreReceiveWithData call on a linked contract. The targets are the recipient account or the token's linked contract and the sender is a system address. The PoolManager is no linked contract and cannot become one without its owner, and a plain HYPE credit to it reverts. The fourth kind, transfers sent in the name of the AQAv2 linked contract and treasury address, follows user flows in size and names only the two addresses fixed at activation, which needs a validator vote. In 1,927 system transactions none targeted the PoolManager, none had it as sender and none came from the zero address, which is the protocol fee controller here (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48).

cleared.check: The protocol fee controller is the zero address. If some transaction ever ran with msg.sender zero, could collectProtocolFees pay out pool funds?
cleared.result: No. collectProtocolFees subtracts the amount from protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). That counter grows only by the protocol share of swap fees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70, src/PoolManager.sol:238), and no protocol fee can be set while the controller is zero (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41). On chain the counter is 0 for native HYPE, WHYPE, USDC and Wrapped USDC. A call with amount zero transfers nothing.
cleared.source: src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call protocolFeesAccrued(address) and eth_getStorageAt slot 2

cleared.check: Work item 1, exits: can an ordinary account make another user's liquidity removal or claim redemption impossible to include or always revert on HyperEVM through gas caps, storage pricing, mempool rules or the big block flag?
cleared.result: No. Removal has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and two mined removals used about 60,500 gas each in the modifyLiquidity frame against a 3,000,000 gas small block. burn and take have no loop either (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and 332-336). The mempool rule of 8 pending nonces and the one day pruning apply to the sender's own account. The big block flag is set by a HyperCore action of the account itself. System transactions do not use block gas. Filling small blocks costs base fee that is burned and rises with each full block. What an attacker can make expensive is a swap, which is recorded in the finding that extends F-039. A pool's own hook can still block removal, which is F-004.

cleared.check: Lead L-219: an Elysium account sends a child chain message whose target on HyperEVM is the HYPE bridge address, a token system address or CoreWriter. Is a HyperCore balance credited to the Elysium Bridge contract, can a later message spend it, and can this move the HYPE that backs Elysium?
cleared.result: The credit goes to the Bridge contract's own HyperCore account and any later message can spend it, and neither step reaches the backing. In a simulated executeCall from the allowed outbox the Bridge sent 1 HYPE to the bridge address, which emitted Received with the Bridge as user, and a call to CoreWriter logged an action with the Bridge as user. The Bridge sends only the value of the message it executes, and that value was burned on Elysium when the message was created, so its 297,189 HYPE cannot leave without an equal burn. HYPE routed this way lands in a HyperCore account that every Elysium account can command through CoreWriter, so the sender of such a message can lose it to whoever sends the next message. No Received log and no CoreWriter log names the Bridge since its deployment, and the Bridge has no HyperCore account. Token escrow sits in the gateway 0xd97B30dE0bA0C2eAeE942afce77530e06c5F122c, which a Bridge call cannot command without the counterpart gateway as child chain sender. cleared.check: Can an ordinary account link a HyperCore spot token to the PoolManager, so that HyperCore sends system transactions to it or reads its logs as token movements?
cleared.result: No. HyperCore accepts a link when the finalizer deployed the contract with CREATE at a stated nonce, or is stored in the contract's slot 0, or in the slot keccak256("HyperCore deployer"). The PoolManager was created with CREATE2 by the deterministic deployer, a contract that cannot send actions. Slot 0 holds the owner. The custom slot is zero and no function writes a caller chosen slot: persistent writes go to mappings and pool state (src/ERC6909.sol:25-88, src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-70, src/libraries/Pool.sol). Only the owner contract could finalize a link, which is a governance act. A linked PoolManager would still revert on transfer(address,uint256) and coreReceiveWithData, which it does not implement, and it emits no ERC-20 Transfer log.

cleared.check: Work item 2, known weaknesses of read precompiles and CoreWriter: audits of AlphaHYPE, dHEDGE and Ventuals and the Papertrade incident of 2026-10-10 show that read precompiles return HyperCore state fixed when the EVM block is built, that CoreWriter actions land after the block, and that the best bid and offer precompile 0x080e can be moved for one block. Does any of this reach funds in the PoolManager?
cleared.result: Not through core. Core calls no precompile and CoreWriter rejects every call shape the PoolManager can produce. A value fixed for the whole block cannot rise between sync and settle of one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). The hazard is for a hook or token that prices or reports balances from a precompile: its numbers lag by one block and its price input can be pushed by a trade on the HyperCore book. That belongs to the author of the hook or token. None of the 307 ERC-20 pool currencies shows a balance change without a Transfer log.

cleared.check: Work item 2, incidents: the reported HyperEVM halt of 2026-04-02, the HyperEVM testnet stall of 2026-11-08, stale eth_call results at one RPC provider on 2026-10-20, the block timestamp mismatch between eth_call and execution reported in April 2026, and the theft of a spot token deployer's signing secret on 2026-11-20. Does any give an ordinary account a hold on PoolManager funds?
cleared.result: No. A halt delays every transaction alike and settlement is atomic inside one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The team stated that the April event was limited to the block explorer. Stale or shifted eth_call results mislead software that quotes off chain and core reads no block field. The token theft was a HyperCore deployer account moving its own supply, which is the issuer class already recorded in F-019. The JSON-RPC page confirms that the official node serves only the latest state.

cleared.check: Assumption A1 once more, given the cycle 2 and 3 critic notes: is there new evidence about transient storage on the validator node, and how far does the archive client's block check reach?
cleared.result: Nothing contradicts the earlier clearance and its limit is now stated more exactly. The archive client executes every transaction, system or signed, through one transact call (executor.rs lines 192 to 213) and compares gas used, receipts root and logs bloom with the header for the signed transactions. Receipts of system transactions are filtered out of that comparison (reth_copy.rs lines 41 to 47). The official replay client asserts equality of all signed receipts and of system receipts when the block data includes them (run.rs lines 217 to 264). A stale synced currency left by one transaction would change the outcome of a later native settle in the same block (src/PoolManager.sol:349-356), and such a difference in a signed transaction would break the replay. Both clients reproduce the chain to its head, which the archive endpoints I used show. The validator node itself remains unread.

The loop stops at the limit and stores the reached price (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344 and 439), so the limit only decides how far a swap that outruns liquidity keeps walking.

cleared.check: Transaction types on Tempo: for legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-7702, the type 0x76 batch with fee sponsor, session credential and authorization list, and system transactions, what msg.sender, msg.value and transient storage look like inside the PoolManager, walked through unlock, sync, settle and take.
cleared.result: msg.value is 0 in every form, because each prepare function rejects value before execution. msg.sender is the signer or a contract the signer called, and a fee sponsor never becomes a caller. A batch shares one transient map and one checkpoint among the calls of one signer, so a sync or a delta can only reach later calls of the same account, and an unlock cannot stay open between calls. System transactions are limited to the subblock metadata call, which is disabled, and the block level calls to CurrentCommittee and to the EIP-2935 history contract. No form lets a second party run inside another party's transient state, and no form credits or debits the PoolManager's TIP-20 balance outside a transfer call.

cleared.check: L-212: can an ordinary account keep liquidity providers out by filling the 30,000,000 gas general limit of every block, given the fee rule and the ordering rule.
cleared.result: Not at a bounded cost. PoolManager transactions do count against the general limit. The base fee is dynamic since T7: 30,000,000 gas per block is three times the 10,000,000 target, so the fee rises 25 percent per block from the floor of 600,000,000 to the cap of 12,000,000,000 attodollars within about 14 blocks. At the cap one full general lane costs 0.36 USD per block, about 57,600 USD per day at 0.54 seconds per block. The pool orders by tip, so a withdrawal of a few hundred thousand gas that offers a higher tip than the filler is taken first, and the filler has to pay that tip on 30,000,000 gas in every block. A withdrawal is delayed only while its sender bids below the filler.

cleared.result: No. Memo passes msg.sender as the sender of the subcall, the EVM refuses a child caller that is neither the helper's own caller nor the transaction signer, and the subcall cannot carry value or run in static context. A contract in the middle of a user's transaction is refused when it calls Memo or Multicall3From. Arc has no sponsored or batched transaction type at protocol level. A bundle is one transaction, and the periphery resets a stale sync before a native settle, as the L-199 item shows.

cleared.check: Do calls that one contract makes one after another inside one transaction meet the same transient map of the PoolManager, and does sync leave its two values behind when the call ends. One eth_call per network to Multicall3.aggregate3 with the calls exttload(currency slot), sync(token), exttload(currency slot), exttload(reserves slot), token.balanceOf(PoolManager), sync(address(0)), exttload(currency slot), exttload(reserves slot).
cleared.result: Yes on all 21 networks. Before the first sync the currency slot read zero. After sync(token) the next call read the token address in the currency slot and a reserves value equal to balanceOf(PoolManager). After sync(address(0)) the currency slot read zero and the reserves slot kept the old number, which is harmless because the native branch of _settle never reads it (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). This is the shape of every contract level carrier: sibling calls of one caller in one transaction. I recomputed the four slot constants from their comments and they match (src/libraries/Lock.sol:8, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-10, CurrencyReserves.sol:11-13). The Multicall3 code on Zora differs from the Ethereum code in bytes and has the same length; the probe passed there as well.

cleared.check: For each of the 21 networks: which carriers put calls of different users into one transaction, and does any of them run a user's calls anywhere other than in ordinary nested calls of that one transaction. Checked: code at the four EntryPoint addresses, Multicall3, Simple7702Account, CoW GPv2Settlement, 1inch AggregationRouterV6, Bebop JamSettlement and BebopSettlement, Across MulticallHandler, three UniswapX reactor addresses, GelatoRelay1BalanceERC2771, the World Chain PBHEntryPoint and the Arc CallFrom precompile; the top level target, the type and the sender code of up to 600 recent transactions with a PoolManager Swap event per network; the verified sources of the EntryPoints and of PBHEntryPointImplV1.
cleared.result: Every carrier found is a contract that calls the users' targets one after another in one transaction, so all of them share the one transient map shown by the Multicall3 probe. EntryPoint v0.6 and v0.7 hold byte identical code on all 21 networks, and v0.8 and v0.9 hold the Ethereum code with different PUSH32 operands (cached chain data). cleared.check: Every state an ordinary account can leave in the PoolManager for the next party in the same transaction, and who is credited what when a later party pays. Walked in the source for the order: attacker calls sync(X) while the PoolManager holds R, then either sends d of X by plain transfer (balance R+d) or removes d inside an unlock of its own by burning claims and taking X (balance R-d); then the victim pays X or pays native.
cleared.result: The lock flag is false and all deltas are zero after any unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:105-113), and take, settle, settleFor, clear, mint, burn, swap, modifyLiquidity and donate all require the unlocked state (lines 147, 189, 258, 291, 300, 305, 310, 322, 332). The only leftover is the pair (synced currency X, reserves R). Inside its own later unlock the attacker cannot call settle without consuming the leftover (line 361), so a lower balance needs claims burned and taken, and a higher balance needs a plain transfer. Victim pays X and calls sync(X) first: the sync stores the current balance (line 286), the victim is credited exactly its own transfer (line 360), and a donated d stays in the PoolManager without an owner. Victim pays native and calls sync(address(0)) first: the currency slot is zero (line 283) and the victim is credited msg.value (line 354). Victim pays native without sync: revert at line 356, which is the finding of this unit. Victim calls settle with zero value and no sync: with balance R+d it is credited d of X, the attacker's own gift, and with balance R-d the checked subtraction at line 360 reverts. A settle never credits one currency for a payment made in another, because the credited currency and the measured balance come from the same slot (lines 350, 358-359, 364). settleFor changes the recipient only (lines 305-307).

cleared.check: How the Universal Router and the v4 PositionManager at the addresses in state/networks.json pay the PoolManager, from their verified source: sync before a token settle, sync(address(0)) before a native settle, settle without a sync of their own, exttload of the reserves or currency slot, settleFor. 77 deployments on 21 networks.
cleared.result: All 77 pay through one function, DeltaResolver._settle, whose text is the same in every verified build: return when the amount is zero, then poolManager.sync(currency), then settle with value for the native currency, or _pay followed by settle for a token (DeltaResolver.sol lines 38 to 48). _pay is a token transfer by the router or a Permit2 transferFrom to the PoolManager (PositionManager.sol lines 522 to 529, Permit2Payments.sol lines 42 to 45), so no other external call sits between sync and settle. No source line calls settle outside this function, none calls settleFor, and exttload is used for deltas, the delta count and the lock flag only. 54 deployments are verified on Sourcify. The other 23 were matched by runtime code after zeroing PUSH20 to PUSH32 operands: 20 equal a verified deployment on another network, and the three first routers on X Layer, MegaETH and Tempo equal each other, with the MegaETH one verified on Blockscout as a partial match with the same _settle. The HyperEVM and Elysium builds use 500 optimizer runs and hold the sync and settle selectors as shifted constants (0x29610465 shifted left by 226 bits equals the sync selector). None of these contracts holds the reserves or currency slot constant in its code. A stale sync therefore cannot change what these routers are credited, and a native payment through them does not revert.

cleared.check: The 0x Settler, the most widespread third party router among recent swap senders (verified as MainnetSettler, BaseSettler, UnichainSettler, WorldChainSettler, InkSettler, PolygonSettler, BnbSettler, AvalancheSettler, RobinHoodSettler and ArcSettler): the same five questions.
cleared.result: In all ten sources the token path calls unsafeSync(sellToken) and later unsafeSettle(), and the native path calls unsafeSync(IERC20(address(0))) directly before unsafeSettle(debt) (MainnetTakerSubmittedFlat.sol lines 8578 to 8588 and 8720 to 8721, and the matching lines of the other nine). cleared.check: The most used third party routers per network, taken from the sender topic of 185 to 9,365 recent PoolManager Swap events per network: do they revert or change their result when a sync was left earlier in the same transaction. Replayed at the parent block with eth_call, sender code overridden with the public Simple7702Account, batch [original call] against batch [PoolManager.sync(token), original call]. Up to two transactions per pair of top level target and swap sender, native value and token input sampled separately.
cleared.result: 209 native value replays and 193 token input replays gave the same result with and without the stale sync, on targets that include the Universal Routers, the 0x AllowanceHolder, the LI.FI Diamond, 1inch AggregationRouterV6, Velora AugustusV6 and many unverified senders. 16 replays reverted in the test only and are listed in the finding. 32 controls failed and say nothing. World Chain and Tempo had no recent swap that carried value at the top level, Tempo because value is not allowed there. HyperEVM gave one swap transaction in the log range read, and its replay was unchanged. Bytecode of the ten most frequent senders per network: 251 contracts scanned, none holds the reserves or currency slot constant, and settleFor appears only in the Angstrom hook on Ethereum, which calls sync directly before its transfer and settleFor (PoolUpdates.sol lines 146 to 148). The sample covers what traded in the hours before the run. A router that was not active then is not covered.

cleared.check: Stale reserves lower than the balance, on the canonical Universal Router: for recent token input swaps the batch [PoolManager.sync(X), X.transfer(PoolManager, 1), original call] was simulated with eth_simulateV1 at the parent block, X being the input token, and every Transfer log was compared with the control.
cleared.result: 12 of 12 test runs that completed produced the same Transfer logs as the control apart from the one unit gift, on Ethereum (6), Arbitrum One (5) and Soneium (1). The swapper was credited for its own payment only and the gift was credited to nobody. Five further test runs failed inside the router call with a token transfer error because the sender had swapped its whole balance and was one unit short after the gift, which I confirmed by reading the balance before the transaction. The reverse case, reserves higher than the balance, needs ERC-6909 claims and was judged from the source only (src/PoolManager.sol:286). Base returned no usable sample in this run.

cleared.result: Soneium: 30 of 30 the same, with swap senders 0xacad7a6ecb6a62bd7f61baab28ac35f4293ab475 and EisenDiamond, all bundles of one operation. Base: 27 of 30 the same, five of them bundles of two operations; the three that differ belong to one account that catches a failed native leg and are described in the finding. cleared.check: Can an attacker that runs later in the same transaction settle to itself a surplus that a victim's token payment left behind.
cleared.result: No surplus exists to take. A payer that follows sync, transfer, settle is credited the whole balance rise and the settle resets the currency slot (src/PoolManager.sol:358-361), so the next party starts from a zero slot and its own sync records the full balance. The canonical routers, the 0x Settler and every replayed router that pays tokens do follow that order, and none of the 251 scanned contracts reads the leftover slots to size a payment. A victim that sent tokens and then failed to settle them would itself revert on a nonzero delta when its unlock ends (src/PoolManager.sol:112), which undoes the transfer. Tokens sent to the PoolManager outside any unlock and never settled can be claimed by the next caller of sync and settle only if that caller synced before the transfer, which the sender controls by never sending first.

cleared.check: Do the canonical routers keep transient state of their own that one user's operation could leave for the next user in the same transaction.
cleared.result: No. The Universal Router stores the caller in a transient locker slot when execute begins and writes zero when it ends (Lock.sol modifier isNotLocked, Locker.sol), and the PositionManager does the same (ReentrancyLock.sol). A revert undoes the write. The maximum input amount slot of the Universal Router is the only other transient slot in its source. These slots belong to the router's address and say nothing about PoolManager funds.

cleared.check: L-259 on the sixteen networks with a trace endpoint: does a take of the whole PoolManager balance that is repaid in the same transaction leave any storage changed, in the token or in any contract it calls. Method: Multicall3 runtime code placed by state override at the PoolManager address and at a second address, transfer of the full balance out and back, state diff of the round trip, the same round trip three times with balances read after every step, and for every token with a clean round trip a one way transfer of half the balance with its state diff. Token lists: the most active currencies of each PoolManager by Transfer logs of the last day and all priced holdings from the balance reconcile sweep of this cycle, the lists of cycle 3, GeckoTerminal Uniswap v4 pools, and every pooled token with a balance on HyperEVM, Tempo, MegaETH and X Layer.
cleared.result: No token keeps a count or a volume of transfers per sender, a cooldown or a last transfer block for the PoolManager that a repaid take can use up. Coverage: Ethereum 304 tokens (304 traced, blocks 26475322 to 26475361); Optimism 108 tokens (108 traced, blocks 159903969 to 159904258); Base 253 tokens (248 traced, blocks 61081750 to 61081750); Unichain 34 tokens (34 traced, blocks 64658362 to 64658362); X Layer 107 tokens (107 traced, blocks 76637685 to 76638664); Arbitrum One 195 tokens (195 traced, blocks 526700807 to 526701162); Robinhood Chain 201 tokens (201 traced, blocks 121133905 to 121139717); Elysium 300 tokens (300 traced, blocks 9752024 to 9752024); Polygon 262 tokens (262 traced, blocks 97800833 to 97801219); BNB Smart Chain 39 tokens (39 traced, blocks 135204514 to 135208099); Avalanche 75 tokens (75 traced, blocks 101130625 to 101130625); Monad 111 tokens (111 traced, blocks 124619495 to 124619495); MegaETH 67 tokens (67 traced, blocks 32609710 to 32610811); Tempo 73 tokens (73 traced, blocks 50372931 to 50374937); HyperEVM 262 tokens (262 traced, blocks 52002201 to 52003492); Ink 94 tokens (94 traced, blocks 61908538 to 61909282). The round trip left no storage change for 2,302 of 2,480 traced tokens. For the rest the changes are of these kinds, none of which can make a later take or payment fail: balance checkpoints that add one entry per block (FXS, LDO, RHUB, PACDAO, PEAK); Aave style tokens, where a full transfer clears the collateral flag of the PoolManager in the Aave pool and updates incentive indexes, with no effect for an account without debt; Compound v3, Pendle, Radiant, Neverland, Benqi and DeltaPrime reward or index updates; rebasing tokens with rounding of one base unit; the deposit timestamp of the PoolManager in the Hop swap contract; the USDG timestamp on X Layer (see finding); holder lists and reward trackers that change for the recipient only. I retested 40 tokens of these kinds with 25 consecutive round trips in one call. 39 succeeded with the final balance equal to the starting balance. The call for uPEG on Ethereum, an ERC-404 style token, ran out of a 45 million gas allowance and gave no result. The one way diff differed from the plain pattern of two balance slots for 111 of 2,281 tokens: storage credit slots on Tempo, holder counts, dividend corrections, reward trackers and tokens that refused the transfer. The only one that enforces a limit is ViciCoin on Polygon (see finding). Tokens that refuse a transfer from the PoolManager are listed in a separate item.

cleared.check: USDG (Paxos) on Robinhood Chain, Ink, Arbitrum One, Ethereum and X Layer: does the reward accounting count transfers or volume of the PoolManager, and can a repaid take make a later transfer revert.
cleared.result: No. On Robinhood Chain, Ink, Arbitrum One and Ethereum payoutGroupIdOf(PoolManager) is 0 and _transfer takes the path that writes two balance words. The traced round trips on Robinhood Chain (17.03 million USDG) and Ink left no storage change. On X Layer the PoolManager is in payout group 2 and only its timestamp field changed (see finding). _applyDelta saturates at zero and the 64 bit conversions bound balances at 18 trillion USDG, so no counter can be driven to a revert by transfers.

cleared.check: Securitize wrappers on X Layer (v4CRCL, v4MSTR, v4COIN, v4HOOD, v4VOLOROST2) and the multiplier tokens BMNRx and ANTx: does a payout from the PoolManager count against a limit of the wrapper or of the Securitize token behind it.
cleared.result: No limit found. The wrappers expose allow list, hook list and wrapper list functions and no limit or rate function. A payout from the PoolManager to an address that the wrapper permits burns the wrapper token and moves the Securitize token from the wrapper to the recipient. In the traced payout of half the v4MSTR balance to 0x10b5b66491d8f91310a85b49cf7a15ef6bbc936a the wrapper wrote its total supply and the PoolManager balance, the Securitize token wrote four balance words, and the compliance contract 0x2fc11ad109c41ab1d347d45d32a31eb3d09e66f6 was called and wrote nothing. A payout of the full balance also updates the wallet list of the Securitize token. Transfers to addresses outside the allow list revert with TRANSFER_FAILED, so an account without Securitize onboarding cannot do the round trip at all. BMNRx and ANTx had a clean round trip diff.

cleared.result: No, apart from ViciCoin on Polygon. ChimeraToken404 tokens on Ink (WIRED, BLOOP, CHIMERIA, GM+) revert with SYNC_LIMIT when one transfer changes the NFT count of a party that has not opted out by more than 64 units. The PoolManager is opted out at initialisation and cannot change that, so the rule binds the recipient of one transfer and a smaller take or an opted out recipient passes. BSTONK and VCAT on Base revert with MaxWalletExceeded for the recipient. In the BSTONK source the PoolManager is exempt at construction and a launcher role can remove the exemption, which is an issuer power. I did not read the VCAT source. BEAN on Base fails only when the test recipient has contract code, and fee on transfer tokens fail on the return leg of my probe because the recipient received less than it tries to send back. The remaining refusals are issuer or author states: IDRX, WRC, CAKE and DogeX on World Chain are paused or locked, Mikami on World Chain answers Sender is frozen for the PoolManager, whose balance is 15,912e18 base units, MOCHI refuses the recipient, RSNC on Soneium is non transferable, rii on Celo has transfers locked, nine HyperEVM tokens revert with InvalidTransfer for every amount, and THBT on Base refuses the test recipient with AccountInvalid.

cleared.check: Tempo storage credits (TIP-1060): the PoolManager has one credit balance at 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 that every user of the PoolManager shares. Can an ordinary account use it up, and what does the next user lose.
cleared.result: Gas only. Clearing a PoolManager slot mints one credit for the PoolManager account, and the clearing refund of EIP-3529 is zero on Tempo. Creating a PoolManager slot costs 245,000 gas more unless a credit is available, in which case the sender of that transaction gets the amount back at the end of the transaction. balanceOf(PoolManager) at the precompile returned 13 at block 50,377,344. Any account can spend these credits by creating slots it pays 5,000 gas for, such as ERC-6909 balances of one base unit under fresh ids (src/PoolManager.sol:322-328). A liquidity provider who clears slots when leaving gets no refund, and the next creator of a slot gets the benefit or pays the full price. No call fails and no balance moves. The same counter exists per token: a transfer to a new holder used one credit of stcUSD (2 to 1) in my trace and a round trip restored it.

cleared.check: Network rules that could throttle the PoolManager address after another account used it: TIP-403 policies on Tempo, resource limits on MegaETH, the reserve balance on Monad.
cleared.result: None of them keeps state per called contract. A TIP-403 policy is a white list, a black list or a compound of three such lists, and isAuthorized is a view that reads set membership. It holds no amount, count or time, and only the policy admin changes it. MegaETH enforces compute gas, data size, KV update and state growth limits per transaction and per block and has no limit per account. The block limit on state growth is covered by F-042. The Monad reserve balance applies to externally owned accounts that pay gas, as an earlier cycle confirmed in the client source.

cleared.check: Rate limited bridged tokens: do xERC20 limits, OFT rate limits, CCTP limits or Superchain token bridge limits sit on the plain transfer path that take uses.
cleared.result: No case found. In every bridged token I traced, a transfer between two holders changed two balance slots only. That includes USDT0 on Ink, Unichain, X Layer, MegaETH, HyperEVM and Tempo, USDC and bridged USDC.e and WBTC on the trace networks where the PoolManager holds them, and the Paxos tokens. AGL is an OFT whose limit of 1.8e19 AGL per send sits in the send path, and its transfer path was read in source. Bridge limits are read in mint, burn and send functions, which the PoolManager never calls (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 calls transfer only). On the five networks without a trace endpoint this rests on the 25 round test.

cleared.check: Lead L-209 and L-332: do the special addresses answer the PoolManager differently when it is an inner frame with another transaction origin? A 69 byte forwarding stub was placed at the PoolManager address by state override and called by 0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0ffee01. Sixteen shapes per target: empty calldata with 1 wei and with zero value, transfer of 0 and of 1, balanceOf(PoolManager) under STATICCALL, the ten IHooks selectors and unlockCallback. 55 targets on Polygon, 75 on BNB Smart Chain, 56 on Avalanche. Each shape was also sent as a top level call with from set to the PoolManager at the same block.
cleared.result: No difference on any of the three chains. The stub and the direct call gave the same success flag and the same return data for every shape and target. The only mismatches are artefacts: the PoolManager address itself holds the stub in the stub run. No target returns 32 bytes that start with a hook selector, so none passes the response test at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154. A 32 byte true comes back only from token contracts (the wrapped native tokens, and 0x1010 for amount zero). Success with empty data comes from accounts without code and from precompiles that return nothing for this input, which is the known case where take debits the caller and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). Value calls succeed at accounts without code, at several precompiles, at the wrapped native tokens and at contracts with a receive function such as the routers, the PositionManager, the EntryPoints and the burn and fee contracts. The caller of take is debited the full amount in each case (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297).

cleared.check: Lead L-261 and L-332: which entry points of the Jenner native code can an account without a role call, can any of them change another holder's balance, can transfer succeed without lowering the caller's balance, and does any CAS20 address report the native BNB balance? Read of cas20.go, cas20_token.go, cas20_admin.go, cas20_asset.go, cas20_stablecoin.go, cas20_permit.go, cas20_memo.go, cas20_factory.go, cas20_policy.go, cas20_activation.go, cas20_errors.go, cas20_storage.go and contracts_stateful.go on master, plus calls on Chapel.
cleared.result: An account without a role can call the views, approve, transfer, transferFrom, permit and the memo variants of a token, the read functions of the registries and, once the feature is activated, createCAS20, createPolicy and createCompositePolicy. transfer and transferFrom debit the named source by the amount and credit the recipient, and transferFrom needs an allowance of the source. mint, burn, seizeWithMemo, pause, updatePolicy, updateSupplyCap and the multiplier setters each need a role. The factory runs its init calls with elevated rights, and those calls act only on the storage of the token being created, whose address must hold no code. transfer returns success only after the debit, except for a zero amount and for a transfer to self. Every successful transfer returns a 32 byte true and never empty data. balanceOf reads the token ledger and returns 0 for an address that holds only BNB. No CAS20 file reads or writes a native balance or calls a contract, and every entry point reverts when value is attached. The millisecond timestamp precompile 0x70 ignores its input and returns one 32 byte word that is constant within a block.
cleared.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/master/core/vm/cas20_token.go and the sibling files named in the check; rpc https://bsc-testnet-dataseed.bnbchain.org (Chapel, chain id 97, Geth v1.8.1, Jenner active since 2026-10-29), eth_call with state override, blocks 144360009 to 144364040 on 2026-11-23

cleared.check: Upcoming fork: what changes for the PoolManager on 2026-12-08 at the addresses that Jenner turns into native code, and can any pool, claim or fee already exist under those addresses? Compared mainnet answers before the fork with Chapel answers after it.
cleared.result: Before the fork the CAS20 range, the three singleton addresses, 0x2007 and 0x70 answer every call with success and empty data. A take that names one of them as currency succeeds, moves nothing and debits the caller (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). sync reverts for them, because the balanceOf call returns no data (src/types/Currency.sol:94), so no credit, no liquidity and no claim can exist under these ids today. After the fork the singleton addresses, 0x2007 and uncreated token addresses of variant 0 and 1 revert on every shape, so take and sync both revert. 0x70 answers balanceOf and transfer with the millisecond timestamp: sync succeeds, settle credits zero because the word is constant within a block (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and take reverts because the word is not 1. As a hook address 0x70 has the flags afterSwap, beforeDonate and afterDonate, and its answer fails the selector test at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154 before and after the fork. The fork therefore changes no balance and no claim of the deployed PoolManager.
cleared.source: rpc https://bsc-dataseed1.bnbchain.org (Geth v1.8.2), eth_call with state override, 2026-11-23, block 135226007; rpc https://bsc-testnet-dataseed.bnbchain.org (Chapel, chain id 97, Geth v1.8.1, Jenner active since 2026-10-29), eth_call with state override, blocks 144360009 to 144364040 on 2026-11-23; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/BEPs/master/BEPs/BEP-706.md

cleared.check: Faces on Polygon: walk of sync, settle, take, mint, burn and protocol fee collection across the two EURe addresses and across address(0) and 0x1010, in every order, for an ordinary caller.
cleared.result: No order credits one payment twice or pays out more than was credited. sync holds one currency and one reserve figure at a time (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). settle credits only the rise of the synced currency's balance since that sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and a native settle is refused while a token is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356). take debits the id it names before it transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). A take or a fee collection of the other face between sync and settle lowers the measured rise and costs the settling caller. mint and burn act on separate claim ids (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). A standing surplus cannot be claimed, because sync always starts from the current balance. The hazards that remain are the issuer hazard recorded for EURe and the dead credit recorded for 0x1010.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork on Polygon: does the dormant Hampi fork or any scheduled Bor fork change what the PoolManager bytecode computes?
cleared.result: No. Hampi has no activation block and its single gate changes only whether SSTORE reads committed state before an out of gas exit. Gas charged, results and state roots stay the same according to the pull request and its tests. Bor master and develop define no fork after Uburu. A fork distributed privately, as Uburu was, could not be reviewed in advance.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork on Avalanche: does Igloo or ACP-209 change what an ordinary account can make the PoolManager do in the next six months?
cleared.result: Nothing is scheduled. IglooTime is unscheduled on Mainnet and Fuji, and its public scope is the move of L1 chains to the Continuous Execution engine. ACP-209 is Proposed without an implementation. If it ships as written, delegated accounts become possible as hooks (the case of finding F-004), and any account could deposit AVAX into the reserved balance of the PoolManager, which contract code cannot see or spend. Neither changes settle, which credits msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354).

cleared.check: Upcoming fork: does the BEP-703 payment lane move balances, pay fees in tokens or change how PoolManager transactions are priced?
cleared.result: No. The lane is one inequality on gas totals per block. It reserves 5 percent of the block gas limit by default, at most 10 percent, for bare BNB transfers to accounts without code and for transactions to contracts that governance lists. A PoolManager transaction is a general transaction and competes for the remaining 90 to 95 percent of an 80,000,000 gas block. The transaction cap of 16,777,216 gas is unchanged, and the largest Quoter simulation of this cycle used 11,518,424 gas.

cleared.check: Can a CAS20 balanceOf call that runs short of gas return zero, so that sync records a false zero reserve and settle credits the whole balance?
cleared.result: No. A storage read that cannot be paid returns a zero word inside the native code and sets a sticky out of gas flag. finishCAS20Metered checks that flag before it returns data and ends the call with ErrOutOfGas, which the EVM reports as a failed call. The high level balanceOf call at src/types/Currency.sol:94 then reverts.
