cleared.check: Lead L-333. Which addresses from 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff hold an implementation today, and what each returns to sixteen call shapes with the PoolManager as msg.sender: empty calldata with 0 and with 1 wei, transfer(address,uint256) with amount 0 and 1, balanceOf(PoolManager), the ten IHooks selectors with zeroed arguments, and unlockCallback(bytes). The PoolManager code was replaced by a 36 byte forwarding stub through a state override and the call came from a separate account.
cleared.result: On all seven chains the same targets do not revert: WETH 0x06 (accepts every shape, returns true for transfer and a balance for balanceOf, empty data otherwise), the four fee vaults 0x11, 0x19, 0x1a and 0x1b and L2ToL1MessagePasser 0x16 (empty calldata with and without value only), L1BlockNumber 0x13 (returns the 32 byte L1 block number for every shape), and the governance token 0x42 where it has code. Every other implemented predeploy reverts on all sixteen shapes: 0x00, 0x02, 0x07, 0x0f, 0x10, 0x12, 0x14, 0x15, 0x17, 0x18, 0x20, 0x21, 0x2c, 0x2d and BaseTime 0x30 on Base. Against src/: a transfer through L1BlockNumber fails the check at src/types/Currency.sol:68 because the returned word is the block number and never 1, sync on it stores a number that does not change inside a transaction so settle credits 0 (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and as a hook its 32 byte answer does not start with the hook selector (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152). The fee vaults and the message passer accept a native payout while the caller stays debited (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295), which is the case of F-048. What a vault does with the ETH afterwards was not read, and the PoolManager has no call shape that could take it back. No interop predeploy (0x22 to 0x28, 0x30) has an implementation on any of the seven chains, so SuperchainETHBridge and ETHLiquidity cannot be called today: a value call or a transfer call from the PoolManager reverts in the proxy and changes no balance anywhere.

cleared.check: Whether any address from 0x4200..0100 to 0x4200..07ff holds an implemented predeploy that earlier sweeps of 0x00 to 0x2f missed.
cleared.result: No. A loop contract placed by state override called each of the 2,048 addresses of the namespace with empty calldata and recorded success, code presence and return data length. Outside 0x00 to 0xff every address on every chain reverted with the 132 byte error of a proxy without implementation. Inside 0x00 to 0xff the implementation slot was read directly. cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Lagoon on OP Mainnet and Unichain (target 11 January 2027). What the interop predeploys will answer when the PoolManager is made to call them through take, sync or a hook call, judged from their source because they are not deployed yet.
cleared.result: ETHLiquidity has burn() (payable, bridge only), mint(uint256) (bridge only), fund() (payable, any caller, reverts on zero value) and setPaused, and no receive or fallback. SuperchainETHBridge has sendETH(address,uint256), relayETH and refundETH and no receive or fallback. SuperchainTokenBridge has sendERC20 and relayERC20. None of the three has the selector of transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address), an IHooks function or unlockCallback, and a Solidity contract without fallback reverts on an unknown selector and on empty calldata. The PoolManager can only send those shapes (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 60-73, 94, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, src/PoolManager.sol:110), so every call from it to these three contracts would revert. This was read from the develop branch and from op-contracts v4.0.0, which may differ from the bytecode that the fork installs.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Lagoon. SuperchainETHBridge.relayETH and refundETH deliver ETH with a constructor that self-destructs, so ETH can reach the PoolManager without a call and without msg.value. Does an ordinary account gain a credit it did not pay for.
cleared.result: No. Native credit is msg.value of a settle call and nothing else (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354), so ETH that arrives by self-destruct gives no native credit to anyone and stays as surplus. An ERC-20 credit is the rise of balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and on Unichain no ERC-20 address reports the native balance. The ETH is burned on the other chain by the account that called sendETH, so the sender pays the full amount that arrives. An attacker cannot make a third party's relay land at the PoolManager, because the recipient is fixed by the sender of the message. Forced ETH was already possible on every chain through SELFDESTRUCT, so the fork adds a second route and no new effect.

cleared.check: Faces of the native asset: LegacyERC20ETH. Walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across address(0) and the legacy id in every order, including the forced ETH route that Lagoon adds on OP Mainnet, public protocol fee collection on OP Mainnet, and zero amounts.
cleared.result: No order gives a gain. 1. sync(legacy) then settle with value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). 2. sync(legacy), then ETH forced in (SELFDESTRUCT today, relayETH after Lagoon), then settle with no value: the settler is credited the forced amount under the legacy id. That credit can be minted as a claim, burned back or cleared (src/PoolManager.sol:310-336) and can never leave, because take calls transfer on the legacy contract and it reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:73, 82-86). The forced ETH stays in the PoolManager as surplus. 3. take of native amount a, then sync(legacy), then a forced back in, then settle: native debt a and legacy credit a. The native debt must still be paid with msg.value. 4. sync(legacy), then anything that lowers the native balance (a native take, or a native fee collection through the fee controller, which the check at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49 does not block for address(0)), then settle: the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 reverts. 5. sync(legacy), sync(address(0)), settle with value v: the second sync resets the currency slot (src/PoolManager.sol:283), the credit is v in native, and a later sync(legacy) reads the balance that already includes v. 6. sync(legacy) and settle with no inflow: paid is 0, _accountDelta returns early (src/PoolManager.sol:369) and the slot is reset. 7. take(legacy, to, 0) reverts as well, since transfer of 0 reverts on chain. One inflow is credited once under one id, and only the native id can be paid out. On chain at block 159909409 the legacy contract returned the native balance for balanceOf(PoolManager) on both chains and reverted on the other fifteen shapes.
cleared.source: eth_call with state override on https://mainnet.optimism.io and https://rpc.zora.energy/ on 23 November 2026

cleared.check: Faces of the native asset: the WETH predeploy, after the sixteen shape sweep. Walk the orders that use the fact that WETH accepts every selector and mints to msg.sender on a value call.
cleared.result: Value is conserved. take(address(0), WETH, a) debits the caller a in native (src/PoolManager.sol:294) and makes WETH mint a to the PoolManager. If the same caller called sync(WETH) before, settle credits a under the WETH id (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364); if not, the WETH is surplus and the caller still owes a. In both cases the native balance fell by a and the WETH balance rose by a, and the caller owes a native. With amount 0 nothing moves and nothing is owed. WETH returns empty data for the hook selectors, which fails the length check at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, so it cannot serve as a hook. WETH has no function that lets a third party move the PoolManager's balance without an allowance, and the PoolManager never approves. This repeats the cycle 2 clearance with the full shape list and adds nothing new.

cleared.check: Faces, tokens with more than one entry point on OP Mainnet: the Synthetix synths sUSD, sETH, sBTC and sLINK, whose proxy forwards to a target contract that reports the same balances.
cleared.result: Same result as the SNX clearance of cycle 2. target() of each proxy was read, balanceOf(PoolManager) is equal at proxy and target, and transfer(address,uint256) with amount 0 and with amount 1 called by the PoolManager at the target reverts with an Error(string). A take under the target id therefore always reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86) and no debt can exist in that id. sync(target) works, so a payment made through the proxy can be credited under the target id, and that credit cannot be paid out. The single sync slot (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32) gives one credit per payment. The PoolManager holds 2 wei of sETH, 30,687.3 SNX and none of the other three.

cleared.check: Faces: the governance token address 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000042 on Unichain, which has no code while five sibling chains hold token code there.
cleared.result: It behaves as any address without code. take succeeds, records a debt in that id and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74, src/PoolManager.sol:294). sync reverts because the balanceOf call returns no data (src/types/Currency.sol:94). No positive delta can arise in that id without a pool that someone funded, so nothing can be minted or settled against it. If a later fork installs code at that address, no claim or credit from before the fork can exist under its id.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Lagoon. Any account can make L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger call the PoolManager with chosen calldata and value. Can that caller identity take funds or leave state that hurts other users.
cleared.result: No. unlock from the messenger calls unlockCallback on the messenger (src/PoolManager.sol:110), which has no such function and no fallback, so the call reverts. take, settle, settleFor, mint, burn, clear, swap, modifyLiquidity and donate revert outside an unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99). If an attacker relays a message from inside its own unlock callback, a take or mint by the messenger records a debt under the messenger's address (src/PoolManager.sol:294, 326) and the attacker's unlock cannot return until someone pays it with settleFor (src/PoolManager.sol:112). ERC-6909 transfer, approve and setOperator sent by the messenger act on the messenger's own claims only (src/ERC6909.sol:25-64), and burn needs an allowance or operator approval from the holder (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). Claims or positions that someone records under the messenger's address can be moved by every account, so that address must never be used as a holder. The owner of the PoolManager is a different address on both chains (state/networks.json).

cleared.check: Lead L-091, first half. Do the sequencer defined gas refunds of Lagoon credit only the transaction sender, and can the credit reach the PoolManager or show up as a balance rise between a sync and a settle.
cleared.result: The specification credits tx.from with refund times effective gas price plus the operator fee difference, and debits the block beneficiary, the base fee vault and the operator fee vault. It applies the settlement after the EVM frame of the transaction has finished. The PoolManager has code and no delegation, so it cannot be tx.from of a signed transaction, and a deposit gets no refund. Because the credit is applied after execution, no sync and settle of that transaction can see it, including through the legacy ETH view on OP Mainnet. The specification is marked as not final.

cleared.check: Lead L-091, second half. What the SuperchainTokenBridge can do to balances of tokens that implement crosschainBurn once Lagoon activates it.
cleared.result: sendERC20 calls crosschainBurn(msg.sender, amount), so the bridge burns only from the account that called it. The PoolManager cannot call sendERC20, because it only sends transfer, balanceOf, hook selectors, unlockCallback and empty calldata. relayERC20 is callable by the messenger only and calls crosschainMint(to, amount) for the recipient named on the source chain. A balance of the PoolManager in such a token can rise without a transfer call and cannot fall. A rise between a sync and a settle is credited to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and it is paid for by the burn on the other chain, as with any transfer in. Read at op-contracts v4.0.0; the file is not at that path on the develop branch.

cleared.check: Lead L-192. Does the parallel validation path for flashblocks in the World Chain node run each transaction on its own journal, and what happens when a result disagrees with the access list.
cleared.result: Yes. At the deployed tag v2.8.2, execute_workers runs a rayon parallel map in which every (index, transaction) pair builds a new revm State, sets the block access list index, creates a new EVM instance with create_evm and executes that one transaction without commit. Transient storage is part of the journal of an EVM instance, so each transaction starts with an empty transient map and no worker shares one with another. The outputs are sorted by index and committed in order into a canonical executor that rebuilds the access list. If the access list hash, the receipts root, the state root or the block hash differs from the sequencer's, the function returns an error and the flashblock is rejected. This path validates flashblocks on nodes that follow the sequencer. The sequential strategy in the same file runs on one State through the OP executor that cycle 2 read.

cleared.check: Lead L-193. Has any chain of this unit moved block execution from revm to the evm2 engine.
cleared.result: No. The seven endpoints report the same client builds as in cycle 2 (op-reth v2.9.0-rc.1-72fcf947 on Unichain, Ink and Soneium, a dev build on OP Mainnet, reth v2.5.2 with base v1.5.6 on Base, conduit-op-reth v2.5.1 on Zora, world-chain v2.8.2). The Base workspace at v1.5.6 pins evm2 at one commit for the crate base-common-evm2, whose README says it is intentionally not wired into the node. The readings of cycle 2 therefore still describe the engine that executes blocks. The question returns when a release notes the switch.

cleared.check: Cycle 2 gap: OP Mainnet had no client reading of its own because the official endpoint reports a dev build.
cleared.result: A third party endpoint serving OP Mainnet (https://op-pokt.nodies.app) reports op-reth/v2.4.2-f863ff4c. In op-revm at the tag op-reth/v2.4.2 the handler calls journal.commit_tx() at the end of a transaction (line 388), discard_tx() on a transaction error (line 457), and for a failed deposit calls checkpoint_revert on the first checkpoint, bumps the nonce, adds the mint and calls commit_tx() (lines 478-491). The workspace pins revm 41.0.0. This is one more released build that follows the chain with the transient storage boundary cycle 2 described. The build of the sequencer itself remains unknown.

cleared.check: Cycle 3 gap and leads L-119 and L-214: can an account without a role cause a balance write on a B20 token, which would change the PoolManager's balance outside its own transfer calls (assumption A2).
cleared.result: No. In the Stablecoin logic v3 and the Asset logic v3 at the deployed tag, set_balance is reached only from move_balance, burn_inner, mint and batchMint. transfer moves from the caller. transferFrom checks the allowance of the source first. mint and batchMint check the Mint role unless the factory is creating that token in the same call. burn checks the Burn role and burns the caller's own balance. burnBlocked checks the BurnBlocked role and that the account is blocked. seizeWithMemo checks the Seize role. A transfer from an account to itself subtracts and adds the same amount. The Asset multiplier is applied in scaledBalanceOf and balanceOfUI only, and balanceOf returns the stored balance, so a multiplier update by the operator role does not move the number that sync and settle read (src/PoolManager.sol:285, 359). What remains is the issuer class already recorded in F-027.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Everest on Base (no date). Does it add a precompile, a token variant or an address that starts to answer calls, which could turn a currency id without code into a live token.
cleared.result: Not in the source as of today. The precompile provider at v1.5.6 maps Denim, Everest and Zenith to the Cobalt set and says they introduce no new precompiles. The B20 variant table on the main branch still has Asset (0) and Stablecoin (1) only. The main branch has B20 logic versions v1 to v3 and no v4. A B20 address with a valid variant that was never created reverts on every call (cycle 2), so no debt can be recorded against it before creation, and an address with another variant byte is an account without code where no positive delta can arise. This answers the cycle 2 lead about a third variant for now.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Everest on Base. Can the PoolManager be named as sender or payer of a Base Transaction (type 0x79), so that the protocol debits or credits its ETH balance outside a call.
cleared.result: No. The executor at v1.5.6 states that before Zenith there is no keystore and authorization is pure secp256k1 recovery, and Base documents Zenith as a gate it does not schedule. Sender and payer are the accounts that the signatures recover to. The fee is taken from the payer before the calls and the surplus is returned to the payer after them. An address with contract code and no private key cannot take either role. Phases share one transaction and one transient map, which cycle 3 already judged. The file has moved on the main branch (HTTP 404 at the v1.5.6 path), so this must be read again on the release that carries the Everest timestamp.

cleared.check: Lead L-195. Which tokens held by the PoolManager on Base and OP Mainnet raise a holder's balance through a call that any account can make, and who may trigger the USD+ payout on Base.
cleared.result: None found. For USD+ on Base, changeSupply reverts with 'Caller is not the EXCHANGER', payout() on the exchange reverts for an account without a role, and the PoolManager holds 112.37 USD+. The probe calls the token contract only. A token whose balance is computed from another contract (an exchange, a vault, an oracle) is covered only if the token itself exposes the trigger.

cleared.check: Lead L-316 for Base, Unichain and Zora. For the most used hooks: does initialize by an ordinary account with its own currencies succeed, and does the hook hold ERC-6909 claims or balances that a callback could move.
cleared.result: Base (sample of 466 pools from 80 windows of 1,000 blocks): the five most frequent hooks, 0xbdf938149ac6a781f94faa0ed45e6a0e984c6544, 0x0469a4bd3724dc86c9542f4694c976da13c450c0, 0xb429d62f8f3bffb98cdb9569533ea23bf0ba28cc, 0x5e320ea6278107968c119942e57d876c5f922acc and 0xbb7784a4d481184283ed89619a3e3ed143e1adc0, all revert inside the hook when an account without code calls initialize with invented currencies, with ETH and an invented currency, or with WETH and an invented currency, each with the fee and tick spacing of a real pool of that hook. Their claims for ETH, WETH and USDC are zero except dust at 0xb429 (4.4e-8 WETH and 0.00011 USDC). Unichain (all 7,811 pools): ClankerHookStaticFee and PrediXHookProxyV2 revert in the same test. UniMemeHook accepts any pool. Its verified source pays the whole fee out with take inside afterSwap in the currency of the calling pool and returns the same amount as delta, so its deltas net to zero in every pool and it keeps no claim or balance. Its referral registry accepts the first 32 byte hookData for a token creator from any pool that uses the hook, which decides who receives 0.1 percent of later volume out of the platform's share and does not change what swappers or liquidity providers pay. Zora (all 73 pools): 62 pools have no hook, and the one hook with two pools accepts any pool and holds no claims. No hook was found that pays from its own claims in a stranger's pool. The sources of the Base hooks were not read, and a hook that rejects a direct initialize may still open pools through its own factory.

cleared.check: Upcoming fork, Lagoon. Relays of cross-chain messages are permissionless. If tokens or ETH addressed to the PoolManager arrive by a relay, who gets the credit.
cleared.result: Whoever calls sync before the relay and settle after it in the same unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). Core never expects a payment to arrive in a separate step: a payer in core calls sync, pays and settles inside one callback. A cross-chain design that sends tokens straight to the PoolManager and settles in a later message would hand the payment to the first account that executes the relay inside its own unlock. No such router exists today because interop is not active. This is a rule for periphery written after the fork and is recorded as a lead.

cleared.check: Lead L-319 on the eighteen networks other than Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Polygon: is there a pooled token where an ordinary account can assign units to the PoolManager that balanceOf counts and transfer cannot move. Method: code of every currency with a balance was grouped by selector set (own code plus implementation behind the usual proxy slots), every function with a name that suggests locking, vesting, staking, granting, minting, distributing, claiming, burning or transferring was called by an ordinary account that had just received a third of the PoolManager balance, with the PoolManager as address argument, and a stub at the PoolManager address then tried to send out the full balance and the balance minus the amount.
cleared.result: No token on these networks ended a trial with a higher reported balance and a refused full transfer. Coverage: Optimism 1594 tokens, 403 families, 7242 trials; Base 9108 tokens, 594 families, 10487 trials; Unichain 4562 tokens, 247 families, 2830 trials; Zora 41 tokens, 18 families, 302 trials; Worldchain 851 tokens, 271 families, 3600 trials; Ink 3438 tokens, 184 families, 2794 trials; Soneium 70 tokens, 53 families, 806 trials; Celo 92 tokens, 43 families, 700 trials; X Layer 96 tokens, 27 families, 512 trials; Arbitrum One 5502 tokens, 1188 families, 20591 trials; Robinhood Chain 738773 tokens, 7616 families, 80866 trials; Elysium 129491 tokens, 577 families, 6606 trials; Avalanche 1841 tokens, 521 families, 9100 trials; Monad 8375 tokens, 405 families, 6452 trials; MegaETH 67 tokens, 32 families, 559 trials; Tempo 73 tokens, 19 families, 237 trials; Arc 261204 tokens, 1143 families, 11682 trials; HyperEVM 262 tokens, 68 families, 934 trials. On Robinhood Chain the 294,326 distinct code hashes were covered through one token per hash shared by more than three tokens (2,156 hashes, 440,634 tokens) and three sampled tokens per code size for the rest (5,551 sizes), so a rare one off contract there can have been missed. Tokens that run as precompiles (TIP-20 on Tempo, B20 on Base) have no selectors in code and were covered only by the full balance transfer test and by the earlier source readings. Limits everywhere: names come from a public signature database that knew 85,092 of 137,912 selectors, arguments follow fixed patterns, and a lock that only takes effect later or needs a second token as deposit is not seen.

cleared.check: Does the PoolManager already hold units that it cannot send. Full balance transfer test: a measuring stub at the PoolManager address (state override, eth_call) sent the whole balance of every currency to an address without code and read both balances after.
cleared.result: Refused per network: Ethereum 1119 of 60024, Optimism 110 of 1594, Base 27 of 9108, Unichain 37 of 4562, Zora 0 of 41, Worldchain 43 of 851, Ink 39 of 3438, Soneium 1 of 70, Celo 3 of 92, X Layer 5 of 96, Arbitrum One 178 of 5502, Robinhood Chain 2439 of 738773, Elysium 14 of 129491, Polygon 104 of 6776, BNB Smart Chain 21 of 3369, Avalanche 20 of 1841, Monad 62 of 8375, MegaETH 0 of 67, Tempo 1 of 73, Arc 115 of 261204, HyperEVM 9 of 262. For the seventeen generator tokens and the two QANX contracts the frozen and locked readings for the PoolManager are zero. The refusals with a price above 1,000 USD are whole balance states set by an issuer or author (block, pause, recipient rule), and the five largest are in the issuer finding of this unit. Others seen: VIBESTR on Ethereum, which rejects nonzero transfers outside its own trading flow, G$ on Celo, BSTONK, BEAN and THBT on Base, PGOLD on Arbitrum One with the message blacklist, PNIC on Avalanche, uPEG on Ethereum where a large transfer runs out of gas and one unit passes, and the Polygon system token at 0x1010. I classed only the refusals above 1,000 USD. On Robinhood Chain the 2,439 refusals spread over 972 distinct code hashes. In a sample of 60 of them repeated one by one, 26 accepted the transfer on the second attempt, 17 refused the full balance and accepted one base unit with a custom error, which fits a limit on the amount per transfer or per recipient and would also fit a locked part, 14 refused every amount and 3 ran out of gas or gave another result. I did not class them further.

cleared.check: Part two: can any transfer start a rise of the reported balance, as an automatic rebase or a reflection does. Test: the PoolManager address sends one third of its balance of every currency, and the stub compares its balance after with balance minus amount.
cleared.result: No priced token gained more than one base unit. Tokens where the sender kept more than balance minus amount: Ethereum 121 of 56331, Optimism 4 of 1550, Celo 1 of 78, X Layer 1 of 96, Arbitrum One 14 of 5247, Polygon 11 of 5574, BNB Smart Chain 27 of 3352, Avalanche 2 of 1768, Monad 7 of 8147. The priced ones are Aave style receipt tokens, stETH, eETH, two tokens named USD+ and xStocks tokens with a difference of one base unit from share rounding. The rest have no price: eight Ethereum tokens of one family where the sender keeps 24 percent more than expected, and tokens whose balanceOf does not follow transfers at all. This test was not run on Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arc.

cleared.check: Part three: public triggers of a rebase on pooled tokens beyond the named ones. For 114 tokens with rebasing indicators on eleven networks (rebase, gonsForBalance, stakingContract with index, monetaryPolicy, rebaseOptIn, rewardMultiplier) the related contracts were read from public getters, and every function with at most two simple arguments on them was called by an ordinary account while the PoolManager balance was measured.
cleared.result: The staking rebase is open to any caller on sVALUES 0x8d8b9044662644e2502e4a6747846f6b0fdaf0bd on Polygon (1,133.70 pooled), on sOHM 0x04906695d6d12cf5459975d7c3c03356e4ccd460 (249.39 pooled), the older sOHM 0x04f2694c8fcee23e8fd0dfea1d4f5bb8c352111f (12.37) and sVEC 0x66d5c66e7c83e0682d947176534242c9f19b3365 (135.07) on Ethereum, and on sT 0x14194a883fc79af1180a9294dff9e6e8d8933330 on Arbitrum One (dust). The fourth word of epoch() is zero for all five, so the next rebase distributes nothing and nothing can be booked today. They join the class of the Polygon finding if distribution resumes. Of the named tokens, sKLIMA would rise by 851,020 base units and sNVB by 54,992,087 base units at the time of the test, and sLGNS, sATH and sSAC were not due. On the vaults of OUSD, OETH, their Base counterpart and Sperax USDs no call changed the PoolManager balance, which fits contracts being outside the rebase unless they opt in. Two Ethereum tokens named Ti have an owner contract with a public poke() that raised the calling account's balance and left the PoolManager balance unchanged. A trigger that needs more than two arguments or a contract two steps away from the token is not covered.

cleared.check: Reading of the claim transfer and burn checks in this repository: src/ERC6909.sol:35-48 (transferFrom), src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22 (_burnFrom), src/PoolManager.sol:322-336 (mint and burn), src/types/Currency.sol:110-118 (toId and fromId), src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59.
cleared.result: transferFrom skips the allowance step only when msg.sender is the sender or isOperator[sender][msg.sender] is true. Otherwise it reads allowance[sender][msg.sender][id] and writes allowed - amount with checked arithmetic unless the allowance is the maximum uint256, so a spender without enough allowance reverts. The balance of the sender is reduced with checked arithmetic. _burnFrom applies the same test with from in place of sender and then calls _burn. PoolManager.burn credits the delta of msg.sender and burns from the named account, so an operator or spender receives the value of what it burns. That is the intended meaning of an approval. mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits before use and transfer, transferFrom and approve use the full 256 bit id, so an id with high bits set can be held and approved and can never be burned. That strands only the holder's own claim. An operator right covers every id and both transferFrom and burn and has no expiry. I found no way in this code for an account without an approval to move another account's claims on any network.

cleared.check: Do the shared contracts that run command lists or batches for any caller hold an approval? I matched every operator and spender address of all 21 networks against Multicall3, Multicall2, Permit2, the Across MulticallHandler, the 1inch v6 router, the 0x exchange proxy and AllowanceHolder, the CoW settlement contract, the three ERC-4337 EntryPoint versions, the Safe MultiSend contracts, the LiFi diamond, the Kyber meta router, CreateX and every Uniswap contract listed in networks.json.
cleared.result: Six kinds of match, all without effect today. (1) The Universal Router is operator of owner 0xd7c7200e8d781013e16db8418ded4767a5beb598 on Robinhood Chain (0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904) and holds allowances from three owners on Base (0x6ff5693b99212da76ad316178a184ab56d299b43, ids USDC, 0x2105 and 0). Its verified source rejects every v4 action other than swaps, SETTLE_ALL, TAKE_ALL, SETTLE, TAKE and TAKE_PORTION with UnsupportedAction (V4Router.sol:34-82 on Robinhood Chain, line 78 on Base) and its Dispatcher makes low level calls only to Permit2, the v3 position manager, the v4 PositionManager, itself and poolManager.initialize. Its token payments use the ERC-20 selectors, which the PoolManager does not have. Its bytecode has no constant for burn (0xf5298aca) or the ERC-6909 transferFrom (0xfe99049a), also in the shifted form the optimizer writes. (2) The PositionManager is operator of one owner on Base and spender for one id on BNB Smart Chain and on Robinhood Chain. It refuses actions 0x17 and 0x18 and has neither constant. (3) Permit2 is spender for one owner on Base and one on BNB Smart Chain. It calls transferFrom(address,address,uint256) with selector 0x23b872dd, which the PoolManager does not have. (4) The PoolManager itself is spender or operator for seven owners on Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Robinhood Chain, Monad and Elysium. It never calls itself. (5) The zero address is operator of one account on BNB Smart Chain and spender on Robinhood Chain, and the native token contract 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 is operator of one account on Polygon. None of these owners holds a claim, and the token contract makes only value transfers. (6) No Multicall, EntryPoint, bridge handler, aggregator or settlement contract of the list appears on any network. These approvals stay safe only while the approved code has no path to burn or transferFrom. The Actions library already reserves BURN_6909, so a later router that handles it with a payer chosen by the caller would make the existing approvals usable by anyone.

The 264 clone proxies (Bunni tokens and Panoptic collateral trackers) were therefore covered through their verified implementations, which check the caller at BunniToken.sol:255-258, CollateralTracker.sol:352-353 and SemiFungiblePositionManager.sol:520-521.

cleared.check: Reach test with debug_traceCall. For 201 code groups of approved contracts (one representative per implementation, chosen by exposure) every dispatcher selector was called from an unrelated account with six argument fillings that place an approving owner, a claim id of that owner, the caller and small numbers in the argument words: 5,388 selectors and about 32,000 traces. cleared.result: 50 contracts have a selector that reaches the PoolManager from an unrelated account. In every burn or transferFrom seen, the debited account is the caller or the contract itself, with one exception that pays the debited owner (redeemFees on Robinhood Chain, see that entry). 33 traces failed at the endpoint. Five approved addresses are 677 byte proxies with a private implementation slot (Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Unichain, Base, Robinhood Chain, one owner each, 4 to 84 USD of claims). The main run saw only their two proxy functions, so I traced the selectors of the implementation through the proxy on Ethereum, OP Mainnet and Unichain (5,350 and 8,926 bytes, with owner and authorized lists) and nothing reached the PoolManager. The Base and Robinhood Chain copies were not finished. This test shows what happened for the fillings I used. A function that needs a well formed struct or a signature before it reaches unlock shows up as not reaching, so the test supports the answer no and does not prove it for unverified code.

cleared.result: No public batch function was found. The 47 accounts on Ethereum were part of the call shape probe. For the nine delegated accounts on the other five networks I sent the 25 execute and batch shapes from an unrelated account with one inner call that must succeed and one that must fail: eight accounts revert on every shape and the ninth returns the same data for both, so none executes the inner call. The delegate 0xb0c75276 dispatches on msg.sender: the PoolManager, the account itself, or an address stored in transient slot 0 by the account's own flow. One handler (selector 0x10d1e85c) runs without that stored address and makes the account call PoolManager.take(currency, msg.sender, amount) with values from calldata for any caller. Inside another account's unlock this pays the caller and leaves the delegated account with a negative delta that only a payment through settleFor or the account's own actions can clear (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 305-307), so the caller gains nothing from this handler alone. I did not decompile the rest of the 24,384 byte delegate. The right of a delegated operator follows whatever code its signer delegates to next (assumption A7).

cleared.check: FeeHookV3 at 0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc (5,116 pools, no initialize flag, both return delta flags, 5.31 ETH held): can a pool created by a stranger move the ETH that the hook owes to creators and partners?
cleared.result: No. The hook has no initialize callback, so any PoolKey can be initialized. beforeSwap reverts unless currency0 is native (FeeHookV3.sol, PoolMustHaveEthAsCurrency0). Every fee credited in ethOwed is taken from the PoolManager in the same callback (poolManager.take of the same amount that is returned as the hook delta), and claim() pays only ethOwed[msg.sender]. Fee settings are stored per token, and only the address returned by token.factory() may register a creator, a recipient list, a partner or a custom fee for that token. A stranger's pool therefore adds real ETH that the stranger's swappers paid and cannot debit another token.

cleared.check: UniversalKlikHook at 0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc (2,240 pools) and 0x07f17023db9cec3f8c6bb53c6940e29dffb0a0cc (1,290 pools): beforeInitialize accepts every caller. Does the hook keep state or funds that a foreign pool can reach?
cleared.result: No. beforeInitialize only stores block.number under the pool id, and a second initialize of the same id reverts in the PoolManager, which undoes the write. The swap callbacks take the fee in ETH from the PoolManager and forward it in the same call to the platform treasury and to the token address. The hook keeps no ledger and both addresses hold no ETH, tokens or claims. This is an older Klik hook (VERSION 2) without the pending fee ledger of the finding.

cleared.check: UniMemeHook 0xb4960cd4f9147f9e37a7aa9005df7156f61e4444 (777 pools) and UniderpHook 0xcc2efb167503f2d7df0eae906600066aec9e8444 (114 pools), no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta: the referral ledger is per account, with no pool id. Can a stranger's pool or a stranger's hookData set the referrer of a token creator and collect or block that token's fees?
cleared.result: No. The verified UniMemeReferral source writes referrerOf[creator] from hookData, where creator comes from a call to the pool currency. The deployed referral proxy 0x3622415b9fcb69b4395d1ad152ea002309c34fed behaves differently: in an eth_simulateV1 run of afterAddLiquidity from the PoolManager address with a referrer in hookData, the RefferalInfo event names the simulated sender (the PoolManager address, which was both the transaction origin and the caller of the hook) as invitee, and referrerOf(creator) stays zero. A swapper therefore cannot write the referrer of a token creator through hookData. In afterSwap the sum of the take calls equals the returned delta in each of the four possible referral tree shapes, and referrerOf[address(0)] cannot be written, so the mismatch case in distributeReferralFee cannot be reached. Both hooks hold no claims or balances. A token contract that reverts on receiving native currency in creator() position blocks exact input sells of its own pool only, which is a pool creator matter.

cleared.check: Clanker hooks (ClankerHookStaticFeeV2, ClankerHookStaticFee, ClankerHookDynamicFee; 0x6c24d0bc... on Ethereum, 0xb429d62f... on Base, 0xbc6e5abd... on Unichain, 0xf7ac6695... and 0xfd213be7... on Arbitrum One, 0x48b8f6ad... on Robinhood Chain, 0xc5d30902... on BNB Smart Chain, 0x94f802a9... on Monad): they hold ERC-6909 claims and offer initializePoolOpen to every caller. Can a pool opened by a stranger take those claims?
cleared.result: No. A direct PoolManager.initialize always reverts with UnsupportedInitializePath (ClankerHookV2.sol line 581). The hook creates pools itself through initializePool (factory only) and initializePoolOpen (any caller, any two tokens), and the PoolManager skips the callback when the hook is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175). All per pool state (locker, mevModule, poolExtension, clankerIsToken0, poolCreationTimestamp) is stored under the pool id. The protocol fee is minted as claims in the paired currency, and _hookFeeClaim burns the whole claim balance of that currency and sends it to the immutable factory (lines 413 to 432). A stranger's pool can only trigger that sweep to the factory earlier. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other addresses returned the same errors in the probe and were not read line by line.

cleared.check: Doppler initializer hooks (DopplerHookInitializer 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 with 244,744 pools on Robinhood Chain, 0xf0d631d54c7e1040ccfa1c2ed737973d6a652544 on Arc and BNB Smart Chain, 0xbdf938149ac6a781f94faa0ed45e6a0e984c6544 and DecayMulticurveInitializerHook 0xbb7784a4d481184283ed89619a3e3ed143e1adc0 on Base, 0x580ca49389d83b019d07e17e99454f2f218e2dc0 on Monad): the hook owns the positions of every pool and holds collected fees. Can a pool from a stranger reach them?
cleared.result: No. _beforeInitialize requires sender == address(this) (DopplerHookInitializer.sol line 497), and the PoolManager does not call the hook when the hook itself initializes, so only the hook's own initialize function, which is limited to the Airlock, creates pools. afterSwap looks the pool id up in getAsset and does nothing for an unknown id. FeesManager stores cumulated fees, shares and the PoolKey per pool id and pays a beneficiary only from fees that _collectFees returned for that pool. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other four addresses reject an ordinary initializer with the same OnlyInitializer error. Pools that an ordinary account creates through the Airlock with a quote currency of its choice were not examined.

cleared.check: AegisHook 0xe449e013004db4a5681e9622ca10c5ba0ea610cc (102 pools): afterInitialize accepts any caller when the fee is dynamic, and the hook mints ERC-6909 claims for its fee and burns them when it reinvests. Can a foreign pool spend claims that belong to another pool?
cleared.result: Not through the hook. The fee share hookFeePpm is zero for a pool until the owner sets it, so a foreign pool charges no hook fee. Pending fees, the per swap fee cache, the runtime data and the reinvest cooldown are stored per pool id, and _tryReinvest burns at most the pending amount of the pool that is swapping. The engine, the oracle manager, the dynamic fee manager and the limit order manager that the hook calls with the foreign PoolKey were not read.

cleared.check: StrategyHookV2 hooks on Zora (0x1f141a2f..., 0x7ae8de96... and two unverified addresses with the same flags, one pool each): initialize succeeds for a second pool with the same currency pair. What can that pool do?
cleared.result: Nothing after launch. beforeInitialize only checks that currency1 is the strategy token. beforeAddLiquidity allows one deposit per hook, tracked in a single flag, so a second pool cannot receive liquidity once the real pool has it, and a swap without liquidity moves nothing and produces no fee. Before the first deposit an account could use the one allowed deposit on its own pool and block the launch, which concerns the deployer only.

cleared.check: Hooks with flags beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta only (addresses ending in 8088, for example 0xf0e1b03731fa1c94b30e90a9a61368e2f5968088 on Optimism, 0x1743c5352f4e11aadb8a6023a10499703b600088 on Polygon, 0x8ca169714fc17174e5c6ef29bf2833f9bdb1c088 on BNB Smart Chain) and the variant with afterInitialize (0x987105e9... on Optimism, 0xc9987661... on Polygon, 0x89fcd097... on Arbitrum One, 0x8d92ff0a... on Monad): initialize is open. Does a pool from a stranger get served?
cleared.result: The first group answers beforeSwap with PoolNotRegistered, InvalidPoolKey or HookPaused for a pool it did not register. The Optimism hook reports version UniswapV2LPHook v1.1.1, stores a Uniswap V2 pair per pool id, and its registration, setPoolFee, setPaused and execute functions revert with OnlyOwner for an ordinary caller. Existing pools were registered by the owner 0x2a315c59a6a95aeeec085c73badac801c2f4209f in a call to the hook. The variant with afterInitialize pairs an ERC-4626 vault with its asset. Its afterInitialize registers any pool whose pair passes the vault check: in an eth_simulateV1 run on Polygon an ordinary account initialized a second pool for USDC and waUSDC, getPoolCount rose from 89 to 90 and pools(id) of the new pool equals that of the existing one. A stranger can therefore register a pool for a vault contract it wrote. None of these hooks holds claims, tokens or native currency between transactions, except 0x60451c7c... on Polygon and 0x92385e5b... on MegaETH, which hold token balances and reject a foreign PoolKey with InvalidPoolKey. No path to funds of other pools was found. The owner's execute function can make the hook call any address, which is an owner power.

cleared.check: Arc hook 0x4ab0bf61327761fffc5910052d9e0b9a94f960cc (1,260 pools, unverified, holds 35.4 units of native claims, selectors owed(address,address), claim(address), poolConfig(bytes32)): initialize succeeds for a second pool of a factory token with another tick spacing. Can that pool reach the claims?
cleared.result: No path found. beforeInitialize rejects tokens that the token factory did not create (NotFactoryToken). In an eth_simulateV1 run the second pool was initialized, poolConfig(new id) still reverted with PoolNotConfigured, poolConfig of the real pool was unchanged, and beforeSwap for the new pool reverted with PoolNotConfigured, so the pool cannot be swapped. The hook has no liquidity callbacks. The configuration function 0x7e19851a rejects an ordinary caller and the token factory with OnlyStrategy(address). Who the strategy is was not established.

cleared.check: HOMIEHook 0xeecbbd7ceb246684b8f621dc9dddca8f72b200c4 on MegaETH (3 pools, no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta).
cleared.result: The fee logic runs only for pool ids that the owner registered with registerPool, which requires the HOMIE token as one currency. afterSwap returns zero for any other pool. The hook holds nothing.

cleared.check: Across the 111 hooks probed on the 21 networks: is there a hook with a return delta flag that accepts initialize from an ordinary account for arbitrary currencies and then returns a non zero delta, or calls take, mint, burn or settle, for that pool?
cleared.result: Three groups do. FeeHookV3 and UniversalKlikHook on Ethereum and UniMemeHook, UniderpHook and hook 0x782d2a5624cfac246fd8f001ccd4d7582a0b8444 on Unichain charge their fee on any pool and pay it out or credit it in the same callback from the amount they take, which is covered above (0x782d2a56... is unverified and was judged from its probe result only). OmniHook 0x03f4051e621ee3f3652adef2c453458a777e40cc on World Chain (14 pools) does the same: it takes its fee to itself and credits five fixed recipients in owed[currency][recipient], so the ledger is per currency and each entry is backed by tokens taken in that currency. The Klik fee hooks are the third group and are the finding. Every other probed hook with a return delta flag either rejects the stranger's initialize or reverts or returns zero for a pool it does not know. A callback that reverted with ManagerLocked in the direct call shows that the hook tried a PoolManager call that needs an unlocked manager, which is how fee taking hooks were recognised.

cleared.check: Leads L-117, L-315 and L-400, answered from the filter precompile, its logs and the client source: what an entry identifies, who adds entries and how soon, whether listed transactions share an address, and whether an ordinary account can make a transaction of another user that calls the PoolManager match the filter through a native take of zero or 1 wei to a listed address, a payment of a listed token, or a pool whose hook or currency is a listed contract.
cleared.result: An entry is the hash of one transaction that arrived through the delayed inbox. The only filterer, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7, adds it a median of 10 blocks before the transaction executes, and the transaction then fails with all gas consumed and no contract code run. 1,389 of 1,491 executed entries name the wallet 0x42607b2e4fde22e83822d4a86ddac58d847dc289 as sender, recipient or calldata argument, and none names the PoolManager or its periphery. A transaction is judged by the addresses it touches itself while it runs. The three levers leave nothing behind that a later transaction of someone else would touch. A take writes a transient delta and makes one call or one transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-80), so a take to a listed address makes the attacker's own transaction touch that address and stores no address in the PoolManager. A payment of a listed token and a pool with a listed hook or currency involve the listed contract only in transactions that use that token or that pool, and the PoolKey names both (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). A swap or a liquidity change on another pool calls the PoolManager, its two currencies, its hook if any, the caller and the recipient the caller named. The on-chain list holds hashes that only the filterer can add. F-001 stays in the operator class. The public RPC node does not apply the filter to simulated calls, so I could not run the levers against the sequencer's filter, and the restricted list and the event rules are files I cannot read.

cleared.check: Whether a claim mint, transfer or burn that names a restricted address can be used to make the filter fail transactions of other users of the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No. mint, burn, transfer and transferFrom write balances and emit the claim Transfer event without calling the holder (src/ERC6909.sol:25-48 and 79-89, src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). The event starts with 0x1b3d7edb, which differs from the selectors of the ERC-20, ERC-721 and ERC-1155 transfer events that the Arbitrum documentation names for event rules. If the sequencer ran a rule for the claim event, a mint to a restricted address would fail the minter's own transaction and no other. The reverse also follows: claim transfers to or from a restricted holder pass the documented rules, which is a matter for the chain operator and takes nothing from other users. I could not read the rules the sequencer runs.

cleared.check: Known weakness on this chain: a filtered message halts delayed sequencing until its hash is on the on-chain list. Can an ordinary account use that to keep other users from withdrawing from the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No. The halt stops the reading of delayed inbox messages and nothing else. On 2026-07-15 one retryable submission held the delayed message count at 35,950 for 4,758 seconds while the sequencer produced 47,314 blocks, so transactions sent to the sequencer, which include every take, burn and liquidity removal, went through. The changelog records fixes for a deposit that stalled the delayed sequencer and for a halt on an already finalized message, and no hash has been added more than twice since. Today a filtered message costs its sender a parent chain transaction and delays the messages behind it by the time the filterer needs, a median of 10 blocks. A user who depends on a forced transaction because the sequencer refuses service is in the operator case of F-001. The live build v3.13.0-rc.9 is not public, so the fixes were read at v3.12.4.

cleared.check: Transaction types, walked for msg.sender, msg.value and transient storage in unlock, sync, settle and take at Nitro v3.12.4 and fork commit 0e44603: legacy, access list, dynamic fee and set code transactions, blob transactions, deposits (0x64), unsigned (0x65) and contract (0x66) transactions, retries (0x68), retryable submissions (0x69), internal transactions (0x6a), transactions on the on-chain filter list, and the message kinds batch, heartbeat, nonmutating call and compressed transaction.
cleared.result: Blob transactions, nonmutating calls, compressed transactions and heartbeats are rejected by the parser. Deposits, retryable submissions and internal transactions end in the start hook: a deposit credits a balance with no call, a submission creates a ticket, and the start block transaction calls only the EIP-2935 history contract after a transient reset. A filtered transaction runs no contract code. Types 0, 1, 2 and 4 and the types 0x65, 0x66 and 0x68 reach StateDB.Prepare, which replaces the transient map, and then one top call whose value the sender's balance pays (a retry is funded from the ticket escrow first). In each of them the PoolManager sees one transaction: Lock, the deltas and the synced currency start at zero (src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38), unlock calls back the direct caller (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), settle credits msg.value or the balance change since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365) and take debits before it pays (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For types 0x65, 0x66 and 0x68 the caller is the aliased parent chain sender. That address holds code on the child chain only if a contract happens to sit at exactly that address, so in practice the callback returns nothing and unlock reverts when the result is decoded, while sync, which needs no unlock, succeeds and its transient values end with the transaction. A set code transaction lets an account with a delegation be the caller and receive the callback, as on Ethereum.

cleared.check: Critic gap of cycle 5: can any transaction type, system call or precompile call a contract with msg.sender equal to the zero address, which is the stored protocol fee controller on Elysium (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48).
cleared.result: No. Signed transactions recover a sender from a signature. Unsigned, contract, deposit and retryable transactions use the aliased caller that the parent chain Bridge recorded, and the zero address would need the caller 0xeeeeffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffeeef, which has no code, nonce 0 and balance 0 on Ethereum and on HyperEVM. Retries use the sender stored in the ticket. Internal transactions must come from 0xa4b05 and make one call, from the system address to the history contract. The ArbOS precompiles do not call other contracts. A zero sender exists in eth_call and gas estimation only. On Elysium setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees are therefore unreachable until the owner sets a controller, and protocolFeesAccrued is 0.

cleared.result: Such an account behaves as an address without code from ArbOS 50 on. From a stub at the PoolManager address, transfer, balanceOf and a plain call each succeed with no return data on all three chains. Currency.transfer accepts an empty return, so take debits the caller and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74, src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). sync reverts, because the balanceOf result cannot be decoded (src/types/Currency.sol:94, src/PoolManager.sol:285), so no credit can arise under that currency id. cleared.check: Known weaknesses, items that cycles 2 and 3 did not list: the Security Council emergency actions of 2024-09-25 and 2025-10-13, the Trail of Bits review of ArbOS 50 and 51, the reports added to the audit index since July 2026, the security note of Nitro v3.10.0, and the security considerations of the compliance filtering documentation. Can an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: None applies. The 2024 action answered a node crash from a crafted Stylus program and a storage opcode that Stylus priced at almost nothing, both availability faults. The 2025 action lowered the WASM stack depth after a divergence between ARM and x86 nodes on the test network, and its report says no funds were at risk. The ArbOS 50 and 51 review has six findings about gas accounting, limits and error handling. The Glamsterdam report covers two pricing parameters and found nothing. The v3.10.0 release note says the release contains security fixes and gives no detail, which I could not resolve further. The compliance filtering page states that a deposit from a restricted address can stay locked in the bridge and that the filter fails forced transactions, which is F-001. None of these changes how CALL, value transfer, TSTORE or return data behave for an EVM contract, and none moves a contract's balance. I did not open the reports on the yield bearing bridge, the tip collection toggler, the one step proof guard and the Stylus permissioned deployer.

cleared.check: sync has no lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 names initialize and updateDynamicLPFee as the only functions that run without an unlock. What can an ordinary account do with that, and which network feature turns it into a gain or a freeze for others.
cleared.result: An ordinary account can set the synced currency and the reserves value while the manager is locked, and nothing else. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers a sync(T) from a plain contract outside any unlock succeeded for a stub T that answers balanceOf with 32 bytes. exttload then returned T in the currency slot and the answer in the reserves slot, the lock flag read 0, and sync(address(0)) cleared the currency slot. The tests of the repository expect this (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41, test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1008) and the test double declares sync without a modifier (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:139-148), so only the interface comment disagrees. A lock check would not narrow what an account can reach. Any contract can call unlock, call sync inside its callback and return with every delta at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). On all 21 networks such an unlock closed and the synced currency stayed in place afterwards, with the lock flag and the delta counter back at 0. A later settle with value in the same call then reverted with NonzeroNativeValue, and it passed once the payer called sync(address(0)) first. That effect is finding F-071 and stays as recorded there. The other network features of the task were walked against the two slots. Code that runs between another payer transfer and its settle: the PoolManager makes no call between those two steps, so such code can come only from the token or from the payer own router. It would not need sync or the missing lock check, because settle and settleFor are open to every caller while the manager is unlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307). A credit captured that way leaves the payer delta open, and the payer unlock reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:112 unless the payer code ignores the amount that settle returns. This is the same on Ethereum. A failed frame: on all 21 networks an unlock whose callback reverted left no lock flag and no delta behind, since the next unlock in the same call opened and closed normally. Transient storage across transactions and inside protocol level batches (assumption A1) was read from client sources by the units of cycle 3 and was not repeated here.

cleared.check: A sync of a native face made before an unlock on Celo, Arc and Polygon, where an ERC-20 address measures the native balance: can one payment be credited under address(0) and under the face, and what does a native payout do while the face is synced.
cleared.result: No double credit on any of the three. One eth_call per network ran the walk on the deployed PoolManager at blocks 83,538,264 (Celo), 32,738,581 (Arc) and 97,822,371 (Polygon), with a funded stub as the ordinary account. With the face synced before the unlock, settle with 1000 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). After a zero value settle cleared the slot, settle with 1000 wei credited 1000 under address(0). A new sync of the face stored the higher balance and the next settle paid 0, so the face delta stayed 0 and the native delta 1000. On Celo a transfer of 1000 through the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 was credited as 1000 under the face id, and take under that id paid 1000 wei of CELO to the recipient. On Arc one unit sent through 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 was credited as 1 under the face id, and take under that id paid 10^12 wei. On Polygon the transfer through 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 failed and take under that id reverted, so that id can be neither paid in nor paid out. On all three the native balance of the PoolManager ended at its starting value and every delta read 0. A native take while the face is synced made the next settle revert with a Panic on the checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:360), which costs the settler and nobody else. An account whose EIP-7702 designator names 0x1010 on Polygon also reports the native balance of the PoolManager, as does any contract that returns the balance of its argument (src/test/NativeERC20.sol:46-48 models one). Such a face gives a credit only for value that arrives while it is synced, and its transfer function cannot move native funds of the PoolManager.

cleared.check: A take of a currency address without code succeeds because the transfer accepts empty return data (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts if the amount is not available. What can an ordinary account do with that, and can a pool, a claim or a debt exist under such an address.
cleared.result: The account can make take report success without any transfer, at its own cost. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers, inside one unlock: take of 5 units of a codeless address returned success, the caller delta slot read minus 5 and the delta counter 1. sync of that address reverted with empty data, because balanceOf is a high level call whose empty answer cannot be decoded (src/types/Currency.sol:94). settle with nothing synced paid 0. mint of 7 units added a debt of 7 and a claim of 7. clear reverted with MustClearExactPositiveDelta. A separate unlock that only took 5 units reverted with CurrencyNotSettled, and one that took amount 0 closed, on all 21 networks. The ecrecover address 0x01 gave the same answers as the codeless address. For the identity precompile 0x04 take reverted and sync stored a constant, so the next settle paid 0. Under a codeless id a positive delta could come only from settle, from burn, from a pool or from a hook delta. settle is closed because sync reverts. burn needs a claim, and a claim needs a positive delta to pay for the mint. Pool amounts are rounded against the caller (an add owes the amount rounded up and a removal returns it rounded down, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288 and src/libraries/Pool.sol:206-237) and a hook delta is subtracted from the caller delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242 and 312), so the deltas of all accounts in that currency sum to zero or less. No claim and no debt therefore exists under a codeless id. A pool that names it can be initialized (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and can hold only positions that need the other currency alone. The only party that loses from the silent take is the caller that asked for it. A holder of a real credit could lose it this way only if the code of a token disappeared after deposits, which needs a token built for that, for example an account whose owner clears its EIP-7702 delegation. That is the pool creator class of F-013.

cleared.check: unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint, burn, clear and sync carry no noDelegateCall, while the test double puts the modifier on six of them (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:58, 151-183). Lead L-423, third item: call them through DELEGATECALL from a stub and say what an account that points its EIP-7702 delegation at the PoolManager exposes.
cleared.result: A delegatecall runs these functions against the storage, the transient storage and the balance of the calling account, and nothing the PoolManager holds is reached. Test on all 21 deployed PoolManagers, one eth_call each with state overrides: a stub P that forwards every call to the PoolManager by DELEGATECALL, and a funded stub E as the ordinary account. Outside an unlock P.sync succeeded, P.settle reverted with ManagerLocked, P.initialize reverted with DelegateCallNotAllowed, and P.owner and P.protocolFeeController returned zero. E then called P.unlock. Inside the callback P.take of 1000 wei of native currency paid the recipient out of the balance of P. The delta of minus 1000 and the unlocked flag sat in the transient storage of P, while the flag and the delta of the PoolManager read 0. P.mint and P.burn moved a claim in the storage of P, while balanceOf at the PoolManager for the same account read 0. P.settle with 1000 wei returned 1000, P.swap reverted with DelegateCallNotAllowed, and P.sync and P.clear ran. The unlock closed, the native balance of the PoolManager was the same before and after, and a second unlock that only took reverted with CurrencyNotSettled. An account D that carries the designator 0xef0100 followed by the PoolManager address gave the same 29 answers on 20 networks. The Avalanche endpoint (avalanchego 1.15.3) executed the designator as code and failed with invalid opcode 0xef, so a delegated account could not be tested there. What such an account exposes: any caller can borrow its whole native and token balance for the length of one unlock and must return it, a caller can book as its own payment any balance rise it can trigger at the account between sync and settle, and anyone can write claim and operator entries into the storage of the account. owner and protocolFeeController read zero there, initialize, swap, modifyLiquidity and donate revert, and no protocol fee can accrue, so collectProtocolFees has nothing to pay. The exposure is limited to the account that made the delegation. The tests of the repository need the production functions without the modifier, because the double forwards take, settle, mint, burn and clear by delegatecall and expects DelegateCallNotAllowed only from modifyLiquidity, swap and donate (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:151-183, test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol:63-82).

cleared.result: unlock from an address without code reverted with empty data on all 21 networks, because the answer of the callback cannot be decoded (src/PoolManager.sol:110). The zero address holds no code on any of the 21 networks, so no contract code and no delegation can act from it. Its nonce is nonzero on nine OP Stack networks (10 on OP Mainnet, Zora and World Chain, 8 on Base, 7 on Unichain, Ink and Soneium, 5 on Celo, 2 on X Layer) and zero on the other twelve. On seven of the nine (Unichain, Zora, World Chain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer) protocolFeeController is the zero address. This unit did not trace which transactions raised the nonce. The open leads L-100 and L-129 ask that for upgrade deposits, and the nonce values belong with them. Arc: the CallFrom precompile lets two helper contracts name the sender of a child call. Both helpers pass their own msg.sender (Memo.sol line 43, Multicall3From.sol lines 43, 58, 81 and 161), and the client rejects a named sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer (crates/evm/src/evm.rs lines 946 to 955) and rejects every scheme other than CALL (lines 895 to 903). A contract that runs in the middle of another account transaction therefore cannot reach unlock or the ERC-6909 functions as that account.

cleared.result: All 21 endpoints returned the same words, the 24,050 byte Unichain predeploy included. Outside an unlock, settleFor, clear, settle, take, mint and burn revert with 0x54e3ca0d (ManagerLocked) and sync(address(0)) succeeds. mint to the stub followed by burn from the stub: unlock succeeds. mint only: unlock reverts with 0x5212cba1 (CurrencyNotSettled). mint to a third address followed by burn from that address by the unapproved stub: unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled, so the burn gave no credit. cleared.check: Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A1 (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 113, 305, 310): can an ordinary account use them on any of the 21 networks.
cleared.result: No path in the text. Line 112 reads the transient counter that every _accountDelta call maintains (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378) and line 113 writes the lock slot; both hold for a caller as long as transient storage lives for exactly the transaction and rolls back with a reverted frame. settleFor and clear carry the same modifier as take and settle, so a locked manager rejects them. The feature that would break these lines is a transaction boundary inside or across user calls (protocol batches, system calls, nested runs with an empty transient map), which is the per network question of assumption A1 that earlier cycles answered from client source and simulation. The reading adds nothing that depends on a network. The cycle 3 critic probe showed on all 21 RPC nodes that these slots are scoped by address and that a second transaction reads zero where simulation is offered.

cleared.check: Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A2 (src/PoolManager.sol:360, 361, 364): a balance that falls between sync and settle, a balance rise credited twice, and a balance reading of 2^127 or more.
cleared.result: As written, a fall makes the checked subtraction revert, the reset after settle means a rise is credited once, and a rise of 2^127 or more reverts in toInt128. An ordinary account can still book a rise that a third party or the token itself causes between its own sync and settle, which is the class of F-041 and its variants and needs no unpinned line. I found no way to use these three statements beyond that class.

cleared.check: Unpinned statements that stand against assumptions A4 and A7 (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 64-74, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166): a currency or hook address without code or at a precompile, and the gas forwarded to a native recipient.
cleared.result: A take of a currency whose address returns success and no data debits the caller and moves nothing, so the caller loses and no one else does; a credit in such an id needs sync, which reverts when balanceOf returns no data (confirmed on all 21 deployed contracts in the probe above for an address without code). A hook answer shorter than 32 bytes is rejected. A native payout forwards all gas to the recipient, which is lever P1 of ASSUMPTIONS.md and was swept per network in earlier cycles (F-021, F-047, F-048, F-049). These lines give an ordinary account no way to take or lock funds of others in the text as written.

cleared.check: Unpinned statement that stands against assumption A8 (src/PoolManager.sol:335): burn takes claims from a named account and credits msg.sender.
cleared.result: burn calls _burnFrom, which requires msg.sender to be the holder, an operator of the holder, or to have an allowance of at least the amount for that id (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). The credit goes to msg.sender, so the only question a network can change is who msg.sender is. A caller identity that the chain forges (aliased cross domain senders, system callers) would still need the holder's approval for that identity. On all 21 deployed contracts a burn of another address's claims by an unapproved caller gave no credit.

cleared.check: Opcode differential on Celo at the production tag: does the client that produces blocks change TSTORE and TLOAD (rollback on revert, clearing at the end of a transaction), CALL with value, CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY, MCOPY, PUSH0, gas forwarding, calls to accounts without code, or precompile dispatch.
cleared.result: No. Tag celo/reth-v1.0.10 takes revm from a fork whose instruction files, journal, call frame and handler are byte identical to upstream tag v107, and CeloEvm::new uses the upstream instruction table for the block spec. The one addition is the transfer precompile at 0xfd, which the PoolManager can reach only as the recipient of a take or as a currency address. Both calls fail there, because the caller is not the CELO token, so the take reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52 and 60-86). The sweep of this cycle shows 0xfd failing on all sixteen shapes. The repository's settlement path relies on transient storage being cleared per transaction (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38, src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:18-41), which commit_tx, discard_tx and finalize of that journal do.

cleared.check: Opcode differential on X Layer at the mainnet release tag: the same list of opcodes and call patterns, read in the revm version and the OKX execution crates that tag v0.0.7.3-rc.1 builds.
cleared.result: No difference found. revm 40.0.3 comes from crates.io and equals upstream tag v112, where the transient map is cleared in commit_tx, discard_tx and finalize, TSTORE fails in a static frame, value moves before precompile dispatch and a call to an account without code returns success with no data. The OKX fork leaves op-revm evm.rs and precompiles.rs without an X Layer branch and its six consensus files are identical between tag xlayer/v0.1.7 and the newest xlayer-dep tag. X Layer changes sit in the handler (fee handling for gasless transactions) and in transact_raw (the blacklist lookup before deposits), which do not touch a call that an ordinary transaction makes to the PoolManager.

cleared.check: A1 on Celo at the production tag: can a value in the PoolManager's transient slots (unlock flag, deltas, synced currency and reserves) cross from the fee debit into the main call, or from one transaction into the next, for a transaction that pays gas in a fee currency.
cleared.result: No. The debit runs inside a checkpoint and the handler clears the transient map after committing it, before the main call (handler.rs lines 616 to 690). The credit uses the committing system call path and call_inner clears the transient map after it (erc20.rs lines 103 to 137, core_contracts.rs lines 211 to 250). The debit and the credit execute the code of a registered fee currency and never the PoolManager, so they cannot write its transient slots. A sync left open by the main call (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) is still set while the credit runs, and the credit pays the sender, the block beneficiary and the fee handler, none of which is the PoolManager.

cleared.check: Can an ordinary account make the Celo node call the PoolManager, or a contract of its own, with msg.sender equal to address(0), by naming that address as the fee currency of a transaction. The protocol fee controller is address(0), and collectProtocolFees checks the sender only (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57).
cleared.result: No. The handler rejects a transaction whose fee currency is missing from the fee currency context before it makes any call to that address (handler.rs lines 509 to 588 at tag celo/reth-v1.0.10), and the context is loaded from FeeCurrencyDirectory, which Governance owns. The calls the node makes with caller address(0) carry the selectors of balanceOf(address), debitGasFees and creditGasFees. The PoolManager has none of the three, since its balanceOf takes an owner and an id (src/ERC6909.sol:17).

cleared.check: Critic gap of cycles 2 and 5: repeat the special address sweep with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, so that tx.origin differs from msg.sender as in a real take, sync or hook call. Sixteen shapes (empty calldata with and without value, transfer with 0 and 1, balanceOf, ten hook selectors, unlockCallback) against the predeploy range, the precompiles, the Celo core contracts, the X Layer system contracts, the EntryPoints and the usual preinstalls, with the stub's native balance read before and after every call.
cleared.result: No target gives the caller more than it is debited. On both chains 248 of 256 predeploys revert on every shape. The targets that accept value keep it or wrap it one to one, as F-047 records, and the caller still owes the full amount (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). No target answers transfer with success while moving a third party's balance: the successes are real tokens that need a balance of the PoolManager, accounts without code, the ecrecover and P256 precompiles and two Celo contracts with a catch all fallback (FeeHandler and Reserve), where nothing moves and the caller is debited (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). No balanceOf answer rises inside the call sequence except where the stub paid. No target returns a hook selector except the identity precompile 0x04, whose address fails isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). The classes equal those of the cycle 2 sweep with the PoolManager as origin, so no swept contract treats the two caller shapes differently.

cleared.check: Lead L-218, Celo half: do the deployed Universal Routers and the PositionManager sync before every native settle, do they treat the CELO token as wrapped native, and what happens to a route that names both address(0) and the CELO token.
cleared.result: No loss path. All three verified sources call sync before every settle. The PositionManager and the first Universal Router name the CELO token as WETH9, and the two later routers name a contract that always reverts. Wrap and unwrap revert, because the CELO token has neither deposit nor withdraw. Nothing needs them: both ids are backed by the native balance, a debt under the CELO token id can be paid from native value held by the periphery contract through an ordinary token transfer, and a debt under address(0) is paid with msg.value after sync(address(0)). A route that names both ids is handled as two currencies. Paying the wrong id leaves the other delta open and unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The guard at src/PoolManager.sol:356 is not reached, because the periphery sends value only after it synced address(0).

cleared.check: Lead L-246: which pools and positions hold the G$ that the issuer froze in the Celo PoolManager, and is a second currency frozen with it because the periphery offers no exit that leaves the G$ side behind.
cleared.result: One position holds 550,000,000 of the 550,022,104 G$: token id 523 in the hookless G$/USDC pool, out of range and single sided, with zero USDC. The other four open positions in G$ pools hold 21,143 G$ and less than one unit of USDm and CELO together. The periphery can close a position and give up one side through CLEAR_OR_TAKE, which calls clear for the G$ credit (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319) and takes the other currency, as F-083 describes. No material second currency is locked behind the G$ freeze.
